US military says it has destroyed 5 Iranian oil tankers after missile attacks on Navy warship. Local Iranian media has reported explosions on Kharg Island, an important site for the country’s oil exports. There are no further details currently available from the reports.

Saudi coordination, empowerment of Yemeni government to reshape balance of power. Political analysts suggest that Saudi Arabia is shifting from containment to a firmer deterrence strategy against Houthi attacks, emphasizing enhanced political and military coordination with Yemen's legitimate government.

Dembélé, Kane and Mbappé headline shortlist for Ballon d’Or, Putellas leads women’s contenders. France Football magazine announced the nominees for the men’s and women’s Ballon d’Or, with winners to be announced on October 26 in London. Top contenders include Ousmane Dembélé, Harry Kane, and Kylian Mbappé, while Alexia Putellas leads the women’s field.

UN condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as fresh displacement wave deepens Yemen crisis. The UN condemned recent Houthi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia that targeted civilian and energy infrastructure, coinciding with escalating violence in Yemen that has displaced thousands of families and worsened the humanitarian crisis.

Police clash with protesters against Trump-linked Albania project. Police in Albania clashed with protesters opposing a proposed luxury hotel project linked to Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner near a nature reserve. The demonstrations have been ongoing since May.

Trial opens in France over deadliest Channel migrant crossing disaster. The trial in France addresses the 2021 Channel disaster, with 14 individuals accused in the deaths of 31 asylum seekers. This incident marks the deadliest crossing attempt to the UK by migrants.

Atletico have work to do to reach home Champions League final: Simeone. Diego Simeone expressed confidence that Atletico Madrid will improve as they aim for the Champions League final at home, despite a slow start to the season and a significant loss to Athletic Bilbao.

Boxing legend Manny Pacquiao takes helm of Philippines’ anti-poverty drive. MANILA: Manny Pacquiao, one of the greatest boxers of all time, was appointed to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s cabinet on Tuesday to lead The Philippines’ poverty eradication agency. Pacquaio is an inspiring icon of success for many Filipinos. Through hard work and exceptional boxing talent, he overcame poverty and achieved global fame as he rose to become the only boxer to win world titles in eight weight divisions. Funding cuts are forcing dozens of health clinics in Sudan to close, aid groups warn. Aid groups warn that funding cuts will lead to the closure of 36 health clinics in Sudan, affecting over 470,000 people amid an ongoing humanitarian crisis.

Nearly 1,100 flights cancelled after UK air traffic control glitch. Almost 1,100 flights to and from UK airports were cancelled due to a technical issue with the air traffic control service, disrupting travel plans significantly.

LONDON: Adidas apologized on Monday after a local Israeli advertising campaign featuring a former Israeli soldier drew criticism from pro-Palestine activists and renewed calls to boycott the German sportswear company. Saudi ambassador meets Croatian envoy to Sweden. RIYADH: Saudi Ambassador to Sweden and Iceland Aseel Al-Shehail recently visited Sinisa Grgic, ambassador of Croatia to Sweden and dean of the diplomatic corps. “We had a constructive exchange of views on matters of mutual interests,” Al-Shehail said in a statement on X. “His kind welcome and good wishes were greatly appreciated.” Meanwhile, Al-Ahsa Gov. Fire erupts at Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab's office located in historic KMC building. KARACHI: A fire broke out in an air conditioner’s outer unit at Mayor Murtaza Wahab’s office on the first floor of the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) building on Tuesday, officials said. South Deputy Inspector General Asad Raza told Dawn that it was a “minor fire”. There were no casualties, and fire tenders dispatched to the site brought the fire under control, Rescue 1122 spokesperson Hassaanul Haseeb Khan said. Mayor Wahab, speaking to the media outside his damaged office, said a “spark occurred at around 9:15am”. “Whether it was a short circuit or something related to the AC, all aspects are being looked into,” he added, noting that wooden objects and a false ceiling further aggravated the fire. “There was no loss of life. The furniture in the room was damaged, but because of the timely action, my chamber, which is adjacent to the room, was protected, and the conference room was also kept safe,” Wahab said. “My room has been completely gutted by the fire, and all the furniture has been destroyed,” he added, clarifying that there were no records or files in his room. “Files only come to me for signatures; I sign and pass orders on them, after which they are sent to the relevant department. If there are any files with me at all, they are only those on which my signature is pending,” he said. View this post on Instagram The mayor highlighted that the KMC staff immediately called the fire brigade and the fire team succeeded in confining the blaze to his room. “Once the area has been cleared, our fire team will properly inspect it, and whatever details emerge will be shared with you,” he said. “If anyone thinks that I will stop working or will not come to the office, that is not the case. I have come to the office today and will continue working from another room. I will also continue making my field visits as usual,” the mayor affirmed. Wahab further said that another fire had broken out at Kareem Plaza this morning, where the rescue team took timely action to extinguish the fire. Frequent fires Fires frequently erupt in buildings across Pakistan due to a mix of poor infrastructure, weak enforcement of safety regulations, and widespread negligence. Many structures lack proper fire exits, alarms, and emergency protocols, while faulty wiring and overloaded power systems increase the risk of electrical short circuits. In Karachi, at least three people suffered minor injuries from smoke inhalation after a huge fire erupted in a factory at the Karachi Export Processing Zone (EPZ), near Landhi Industrial Area on Monday. The blaze destroyed half of the three-storey unit and badly damaged other factories. Another massive fire had broken out at the city’s Gul Plaza shopping mall on the night of Jan 17 and claimed at least 73 lives . The blaze took nearly two days to be fully extinguished and left over 1,100 shops in ruins. In early February, a massive fire in a plastic factory at Landhi EPZ engulfed several nearby factories, and it took 13 hours of efforts to bring it under control. Days later, a fire erupted in a high-rise building near Karachi’s Baloch Colony on Feb 12, with around 150 people evacuated . On Feb 17, a fire had also erupted at a chemical factory in the SITE Industrial Area. The next month, a blaze that broke out in Imtiaz Superstore’s Zamzama branch was brought under control after hours-long efforts by rescue officials. In June, hundreds of people were evacuated as a fire erupted in the cold storage of a department store situated in a mega shopping mall on Rashid Minhas Road in Federal B Area.

IHC forms larger bench to hear plea against PTI's Sept 27 protest. ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Tuesday decided to form a larger bench to hear a petition against the PTI’s planned Sept 27 protest, terming the matter sensitive and observing that it could have constitutional implications. The IHC also issued notices to the police chiefs of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Balochistan, among other officials, seeking their attendance at the next hearing on Sept 10. The PTI has announced a nationwide protest on Sept 27 to demand the release of party founder Imran Khan and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. A citizen, Waqas Ahmed, had challenged the planned move in the IHC on the grounds that the protest could disrupt routine life, traffic and business activities in the federal capital. Chief Justice Sardar Muhammad Sarfaraz Dogar took up the plea on Tuesday, with the petitioner’s lawyer, Akhter Cheena, informing the court that his client was a trader in Islamabad and would be “directly affected” by the planned protest. When the IHC CJ asked how the petitioner would be affected, the lawyer replied that the protest had been announced by KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, who planned to lead the demonstration in Islamabad. This could disrupt businesses and normal life in the capital, he explained. The lawyer also read out newspaper clippings containing statements attributed to the KP CM and argued that several cases against PTI leaders were already pending in courts. “All these cases have to be decided according to law,” the lawyer stressed, arguing that if pressure through street protests was accepted as a means of obtaining relief in one case, people across the country with cases pending in court could use the same means. He also voiced concerns about the possibility of an attack on Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail — where Imran is incarcerated — asking whether a plan similar to the May 9, 2023 attack at the General Headquarters in Rawalpindi could be carried out. Terming the planned protest “illegal”, he recalled the November 2024 protest by the PTI. November 26 protests , as they famously came to be known as, saw more than 10,000 PTI protesters surge into Islamabad, defying a ban on public gatherings and a lockdown to skirmish with 20,000 security forces enlisted to turn them back. A day of clashes between security forces and protesters in the city’s Red Zone had ended in the PTI leadership’s hasty retreat. Lawyer Cheena noted that casualties were also reported in the incident. He said three Rangers personnel had lost their lives and questioned how that happened if the claims that the protesters were unarmed were true. Citing media reports, he said the protest caused losses of around Rs240 million. He argued that political pressure “should not be used to get judicial relief”. “The only purpose [of the Sept 27 protest] is to exert pressure and obtain relief,” the counsel alleged. The lawyer contended that the Constitution allowed the government to impose “lawful restrictions” on protests. He referred to the legal framework governing protests in Islamabad and questioned whether the protesters would enter the federal capital on Sept 27 with government machinery with them. At that, CJ Dogar repeated the question, asking whether the protesters would have the KP government’s machinery. The counsel claimed that they would and produced before the court a letter dated Nov 21, 2024, issued by the Ministry of Interior. He argued that despite the federal government’s communication, government machinery had allegedly been used during the 2024 protest. The lawyer further claimed that, so far, no application had been submitted before the Islamabad district magistrate, seeking permission for the planned protest. He further contended that Imran was a convicted prisoner and that two cases concerning him were pending before the IHC. He also read out the orders passed in the £190m Al-Qadir Trust case and argued that the court had repeatedly asked Imran’s counsel to advance arguments on the appeal against his conviction, but arguments had not been concluded. “This is his position in a legal matter before this court,” the counsel said. He then questioned whether the government could direct a court to suspend a sentence in an appeal merely because two million people came out in support of the convict. “Can the government direct the court to suspend the sentence in an appeal? Is this possible?” the counsel asked and asserted that the Constitution clearly provided for the independence of the judiciary. Referring to political developments in other provinces, the counsel said a march had also taken place in Sindh, and KP authorities had announced that facilities would be provided to the protesters. He again argued that the courts could issue guidelines regarding protests, but such arrangements could not be used to provide relief to individuals facing criminal cases. After hearing the initial arguments, CJ Dogar observed that the matter was sensitive and had constitutional implications. Subsequently, the court decided to constitute a larger bench to hear the petition, comprising CJ Dogar, Justice Muhammad Azam Khan and Justice Muhammad Asif. It also issued notices to the relevant parties, including the attorney general for Pakistan; chief secretaries and inspectors general (IG) of KP, Punjab and Balochistan; as well as the chief commissioner, deputy commissioner and IG of Islamabad. The court summoned these officials in their personal capacity. Notices were also issued to the advocates general of KP, Punjab and Balochistan, along with the Islamabad prosecutor general.

Houthi attacks disrupt Saudi energy facilities, wound 73, authorities say. Operations at some energy facilities in Saudi Arabia, the world’s top oil exporter, were halted on Tuesday following attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels that wounded 73 people, in what Saudi authorities described as a dangerous escalation. Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry strongly condemned the “terrorist Houthi militia’s targeting of civilian and economic” sites in the southern cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, and Najran. The ministry said the attacks resulted in 73 civilians being injured, including women and children. Fires erupted at the sites and several people were injured as firefighting and other emergency teams rushed to contain the blazes and assess the damage, the Saudi energy ministry said. It added that the authorities concerned were dealing with the repercussions of the attacks. “The needed measures will be taken to ensure the safety of the facilities and workers and the continuation of work according to the approved operational plans,” said the ministry. The Saudi foreign ministry said Riyadh would “take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty”. It also called for an “immediate halt to all forms of escalation practised by this militia”, as well as Houthi attacks on shipping. The flare-up in violence between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis came as tensions mounted between the United States and Iran as the wider Middle East conflict sent oil prices soaring with diplomatic negotiations stalling. Brent crude futures rose $1 to $98 per barrel after the Saudi energy ministry statement, while US crude futures rose over $2 to $93.65 per barrel. On Monday, the Financial Times said Aramco’s Jazan oil facilities were hit in new strikes, and the damage was being assessed. Reuters was not immediately able to verify the report and Aramco has not commented. The Houthi military spokesperson said the group will announce in the coming hours a broad operation deep into Saudi territory. Spokesperson Yahya Saree said on Monday that Riyadh had taken “escalatory steps” by conducting airstrikes on Yemen. The Saudi-led coalition did not announce any recent strikes on Yemen, but the Yemeni government has in recent days mounted an offensive on multiple fronts against the Houthis in Yemen. The coalition vowed to respond firmly to the latest outbreak of hostilities , saying the latest escalation against the de facto Opec leader was “dangerous”. “The coalition will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confront its hostile approach,” Colonel Turki al-Malki said in a statement on X. The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks towards Saudi Arabia since they declared a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting its vessels in the Red Sea. Pakistan condemns attack After the latest attack, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif issued a condemnation and expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. “I condemn in the strongest terms the cowardly attack by Houthis targeting civilian and energy facilities in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, which have left many people injured,” he posted on X. The premier added that Pakistan stood in “unwavering solidarity” with the leadership and people of Saudi Arabia. “Such dastardly attacks threaten innocent lives as well as regional peace and security. We reaffirm our steadfast support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity, and pray for the swift recovery of all those injured,” he concluded. Meanwhile, the Foreign Office issued a statement condemning, in the strongest possible terms, the “reprehensible” attacks carried out by the Yemeni Houthis against targets in Saudi Arabia. Terming the attacks “a flagrant violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the kingdom”, the FO added that they threaten peace and stability in the region and undermine efforts to ensure a peaceful and durable resolution of the conflict in Yemen. “Pakistan reiterates its unwavering support for the sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and prosperity of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and stands in complete solidarity with the leadership, Government and brotherly people of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” the FO said, conveying Pakistan’s wishes for the swift and full recovery of those injured in the attacks. “Consistent with the UN Charter and international law, Pakistan fully supports the kingdom’s legitimate right to take all necessary measures to defend its territory, protect its citizens and residents and safeguard its national assets against any threat,” the statement read. “Pakistan has been and will continue to make all efforts for achieving lasting peace and stability in the region.” Pakistan had condemned previous Houthis’ threats to Saudi Arabia and to trading with the kingdom via the Red Sea. It also warned that it had the right to self-defence if its “maritime interests” were targeted in “any hostile act”. In late July, Saudi Arabia unveiled plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition to protect shipping and energy supply routes in the Red Sea. Fourteen countries, including Pakistan, had voiced support for the coalition. Last month, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye also signed a joint defence agreement under which an attack against one of them would be treated as an attack against all of them. The Yemeni threat to shipping and Saudi oil facilities comes in parallel with Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz , which has become the central flashpoint between Tehran and Washington amid efforts to end the Middle East war begun by the US and Israel in February.

Babar says was surprised by PCB’s decision to sack Sarfraz, send seven players home. The Pakistan Cricket Board’s (PCB) decision to sack the national team’s head coach and send seven players back home following the defeat against England at Lord’s last week came as a surprise to captain Babar Azam, he revealed on Tuesday. The 194-run drubbing — which sealed the three-match series for the hosts — was followed by Sarfraz Ahmed’s removal as Pakistan’s head coach and Umar Gul’s dismissal as bowling coach. They were replaced by white-ball head coach Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke, respectively. Seven players, including seasoned campaigners Imam-ul-Haq, Mohammad Rizwan and Salman Ali Agha, were axed from the squad midway through the series, while five of the replacements flown to the UK were uncapped players. The wholesale changes, as it emerged later, were planned outside the Pakistan dressing room by the national selection panel. As was the case with most members of the team’s contingent, the developments came as a surprise to Babar as well. “It was news to me as well,” Babar said during the pre-match press conference ahead of the final Test at Edgbaston. “I only found out about these things later.” Following the PCB’s dramatic move, the board’s high-performance director and selector Aaqib Javed revealed that the decision to sack the coaching staff was a reaction to their inability to make certain selection calls ahead of the second Test. While Sarfraz and Umar bore the brunt of the PCB’s action, Babar was retained to lead the side in the final Test. The captain, however, distanced himself from the board’s decisions. Pakistan’s Azan Awais during practice ahead of the third Test match against England at Edgbaston, Birmingham, England on September 7, 2026. — Reuters “But as I said, the PCB made the decisions, so I think they would be better placed to explain them,” he said. “Whatever decision the PCB has taken, as a player and as captain, I have to go along with the decision made by the cricket board. “…The PCB would have made its decision after giving it considerable thought. “In my opinion, it would be better to ask them about it because they would be able to explain it much better.” Babar also gave a straight “no” when asked whether he was aware of the PCB’s internal inquiry into the discipline and conduct of certain players. Nothing to lose Babar and his players have little option but to put a tumultuous week behind them and focus on what they can produce on the field. To do so, however, he and Hesson have a number of fresh faces to choose from. The uncapped duo of pacer Razaullah and all-rounder Arafat Minhas could make their debuts, while Saim Ayub — who has eight Tests to his name — is likely to return to the side. Babar described the situation as an opportunity for the young players amid the chaos. England’s Jamie Smith during practice ahead of the third Test match against England at Edgbaston, Birmingham, England on September 7, 2026. — Reuters “…The new players are coming in, and they have a golden opportunity to grab it and play this game,” he said, adding that the final Test, being a dead rubber, could help Pakistan handle the pressure better. “For us, this is an opportunity as a team and as a group. The series is lost, but we have nothing to lose. So we can play freely, go out onto the ground and believe in ourselves as a team,” he added. “We have had a couple of days of practice and have spoken to each other a lot. Whenever a new team or a youngster comes in, there is a little excitement, and that excitement is visible.”

PM Shehbaz seeks input from business community as he stresses export-led growth. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday sought recommendations from industrialists and businesspeople on how to increase export-led growth in the country. “Whatever growth we have to achieve, it has to be export-led growth, period,” the premier remarked while addressing a meeting with prominent leaders of the business community. He added that any other kind of growth had “no meaning” and reinforced that economic growth had to be export-led. “Today’s meeting is because we’re in the first quarter, in the month of September. I need your opinions on how to increase our exports, as well as what challenges we will face and how to address them,” PM Shehbaz said. The prime minister gave the example of special tax relief to exporters as a means to achieve this growth. He recalled that in the run-up to the federal budget presented in June this year, the government held multiple meetings and had “intense consultations” with the business community. “Through your consultations in difficult times, the way we brought structural changes over the past two-and-a-half years … it’s teamwork. It’s a tremendous teamwork,” PM Shehbaz said. “As a result, we made overdue structural reforms. It’s a long journey, but through enforcement we recovered Rs800 billion in one year. No new taxes were imposed.” PM Shehbaz praised the teamwork involved between the business community and the government, adding that Pakistan was ready to pursue growth with their input. In July, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said the government was pursuing a strategy to diversify exportable products and market portfolios to achieve a target of six per cent sustainable economic growth. “Our destination is not only stabilisation but sustainable growth of at least 6pc. That growth has to be export-led; otherwise it will become another economic bubble that bursts within a few years,” he said. Last Monday, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb said that the government’s focus was on building an ecosystem to support sustainable growth that was led by the private sector and export-driven. The minister said Pakistan had moved from stabilisation towards growth, but the key challenge now was to ensure its sustainability. Earlier this week, PM Shehbaz welcomed the launch of export insurance coverage by the Export Development Fund (EDF) and the Export-Import Bank of Pakistan, saying the facility would help small and medium enterprises (SMEs) expand the country’s exports. Chairing a meeting on the EDF, he said the Rs3bn risk pool would expand access to export credit insurance, especially for SMEs, and help the business community increase export volumes. He described the initiative as a highly welcome step to promote small and medium-sized businesses and strengthen the national economy.

Govt minimises commercial banks' role in pension payments. ISLAMABAD: The finance ministry on Tuesday eliminated the administrative role of commercial banks in the biometric verification and validation of proof-of-life certificates (PoLCs), in a move aimed at facilitating pensioners. The government also directed that pensioners’ bank accounts would not be subject to account dormancy requirements. The Ministry of Finance issued revised standard operating procedures (SOPs) to enable digital proof-of-life certificates (PoLCs) and pension disbursements on the directives of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. “The federal government has formally eliminated the role of commercial banks in carrying out standard banking biometric verification or PoLC validation for pensioners,” the finance ministry said in its notification. Instead, the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) has been integrated with the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) and Military Accountant General (MAG) via a secure application programming interface (API). “The Digital Life Signal is transmitted directly from Nadra to CGA/MAG, bypassing commercial banking channels,” the notification said. It added that under the new SOPs, commercial banks would serve solely as “pension disbursement agencies” and would have no statutory or administrative role in the verification, collection, retention or validation of PoLCs or biometric data under ordinary circumstances. The only exception would be when they act strictly as an authorised operational conduit through Nadra’s designated system for generating PoLCs. “Furthermore, no pension-disbursing account of a pensioner shall be rendered dormant by the bank for the purpose of processing or disbursing pension payments,” the notification declared, adding that these SOPs superseded all previous SOPs. It also formally abolished the physical “Disburser’s Half” process — paper documentation previously used for pension payments. Federal pensions will now be disbursed exclusively through the Direct Credit System (DCS). The revised SOPs were developed in consultation with all stakeholders, including the State Bank of Pakistan, Accountant General Offices, Nadra and the finance ministry, to facilitate pensioners through a more convenient mechanism while strengthening verification. The notification explained that pensioners’ accounts would no longer be marked as dormant, as already decided last month, for the purposes of the Federal Government Receipt and Payment Rules, 2025. “Standard bank dormancy requirements are non-applicable to pension accounts,” the order said. To enable the revised digital verification mechanism, pensioners would be able to complete PoLC verification via the Nadra PakID mobile app or authorised Nadra channels like Nadra Registration Centers, Mobile Units, e-Sahulat franchises or bank branches operating strictly as Nadra PoLC centers. However, the pensioners would have to ensure biannual verification. “Verification must occur at least once every six months or 180 days,” replacing the existing system of a bi-annual schedule fixed for March and September. “Pensioners may verify at any time within the 180-day interval”, it explained. Family pensioners drawing pensions, subject to marital status conditions, must submit Form-12 declarations as required. The notification said account transfers must be routed through the target scheduled bank, while overpayments or discrepancies must be reported directly to the relevant accounts office and the bank. The SOPs also provided two options for activating dormant pensioners’ accounts: either undergoing biometric verification through Nadra’s system hosted at bank branches serving as PoLC verification centres, or receiving a pension credit from the CGA/MAG from September 2026 onwards. Pension rolls will be generated by the 24th and verified by the 26th of each month for execution through the SBP’s RAAST or other micropayment channels. This will be subject to quarterly audits and reconciliation of Nadra logs. The ministry has also directed banks to open pensioners’ accounts solely in the name of the pensioner or eligible family pensioner, prohibiting joint accounts. Banks are not allowed to collect, retain, accept or verify physical life certificates or pensioners’ biometric data in their ordinary banking capacity for pension accounts. Banks also cannot compel pensioners to visit branches for biometric verification of pension accounts for standard PoLC purposes. On the other hand, if a pensioner approaches a branch with paper documentation, the bank shall direct them to the Nadra Pak-ID app or a designated Nadra registration centre and shall not collect, retain or process such documentation. Under no circumstances can a bank place a pension account on dormant status, for the purposes of the Federal Government Receipt and Payment Rules, 2025. “Banks shall not impose debit restrictions due to non-submission of proof of life to the bank.” The banks have been directed to reactivate accounts marked dormant before August 22, 2026, either following Nadra verification at an authorised branch conduit or upon confirmation of pension receipt from CGA/MAG from September 2026 onwards. Moreover, if an account was placed in ‘suspense status’ by CGA/MAG and funds remained uncollected, banks would remit the funds to the government upon receipt of formal notice from the CGA. Banks shall not independently suspend or close accounts. For pensioners unable to use the Pak-ID mobile app due to lack of digital access, advanced age or debilitating medical conditions, or in family pension cases where real-time data regarding remarriage or marital status has not been updated in Nadra records, individuals may visit a designated District Accounts Office or Pension Facilitation Centre under CGA/MAG to submit a manual life certificate (Form 10) or declaration (Form 12) regarding remarriage or marital status. In such cases, authorised personnel would upload the documents directly into the centralised system, and “commercial banks are strictly prohibited from accepting or processing Form 10 or Form 12 directly”, the notification said. Finally, quarterly reconciliations shall be carried out between accounts offices and banks based on API logs and digital ledgers. Discrepancies would be resolved within six weeks.

UK's Miliband announces sanctions on goods from West Bank over 'ethnic cleansing' by Israeli settlers. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on Tuesday accused the Israeli government of turning a “blind eye” to what he called “ethnic cleansing” by settlers in the West Bank. In a video statement, he called the situation in Palestine a “moral emergency” and said that there is increasing evidence of war crimes in Gaza. “We are witnessing unprecedented settler terrorism in the West Bank,” he said. “The British government has come to the same conclusion as the former prime minister of Israel and others, that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.” He noted that Tel Aviv had not only ignored these developments, but that members and officials had made statements or taken actions enabling the forced displacement of Palestinians. “We will not stand by. We’re going to be stronger in standing up for what is right, and bolder in the action we take,” Miliband said, adding that London’s north star was the two-state solution. “Today, we are calling out the occupation of Palestine as unlawful,” he added. “We are banning the import of goods from illegal settlements, we’re taking action on services to target those who finance, facilitate or construct new settlements, and we’re banning advertisements of settlement properties and land.” In parliament today, Miliband said the British government would introduce “an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories”, in a move coordinated with other countries. “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists,” said Miliband. He also announced that Britain would “take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion” and that the measures would be in place within six to nine months. Miliband added that the UK was sanctioning “a further set of extremist settlers who have supported or incited acts of violence against Palestinian communities”. Miliband, the son of Jewish refugees to Britain, said he was “proud” of his Jewish heritage and was “unwavering” in his support of Israel. “There is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the State of Palestine,” he added. US will not join sanctions on Israeli settlements US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States will not join the UK-led sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements, and that it does not want anything to destabilise the West Bank. “Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did,” Rubio told journalists about the sanctions before departing on a trip to Latin America, adding: “We don’t want to see anything destabilising going on right now in the West Bank with so much going on in the region.” UK, France among 12 countries sanctioning Israeli settlements Twelve countries, including the UK, Canada and France, said they would slap sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after increasing attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the occupied territory. Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden also plan to limit trade with the settlements, the nations’ foreign ministers said in a joint statement . Ireland and Spain have already taken measures against trade with Israeli settlements, and France has for weeks been pushing for a similar decision from the European Union , Israel’s leading trading partner, but has been blocked by some members. “The government of Israel’s actions in the West Bank are undermining the possibility of a two-state solution,” the 12 ministers said, referring to a plan under which two states — one Israeli and one Palestinian — would live peacefully side by side. Israeli soliders gather during a military operation after a Palestinian man barricaded himself inside a home in the Israel-occupied West Bank village of Aqraba, south of the city of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank on September 8, 2026. — AFP “The situation is rapidly deteriorating amid unprecedented levels of settler violence and settlement expansion,” they warned. “The government of Israel must immediately halt the expansion of settlements and civilian administrative powers, ensure accountability for settler violence, and investigate allegations against Israeli forces.” The ministers said the 12 countries “confirm their intention to introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with settlements which are illegal under international law, or that they are actively considering these and other measures, in accordance with their national procedures.” Israeli court rejects petition to halt key settlement project An Israeli court rejected a bid from rights groups to halt the development of a settlement in the occupied West Bank that would severely undermine the territorial contiguity of a future Palestinian state. The Jerusalem District Court said in a ruling it had dismissed the motion, which aimed to stall the publication of tenders for the settlement east of Jerusalem. Israel’s construction and housing ministry opened a tender for construction of more than 1,200 housing units in July , leading NGOs to file motions against it. An image taken from the Israeli-occupied West Bank village of Aqraba shows the the new illegal Israeli outpost (C) being built on Palestinian land and sandwiched between Aqraba and Jurish (on the hill), south of the West Bank city of Nablus on September 8, 2026. — AFP The E1 plan — approved by Israel last year after decades of being frozen, notably due to pressure from successive US administrations — would further isolate Israeli-occupied east Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank. Six European countries, including the UK and France, called on Israel to halt the project in August. The Israeli judge ruled that “no irreversible physical changes are imminent, and adequate legal safeguards are in place” for the development project, arguing that courts could bring a permanent ruling on the project as a whole, well before physical construction begins on the ground. The petitioners, including Israeli NGO Peace Now, had argued that the project would lead to the eviction of hundreds of Palestinians. “The court’s decision plays into the government’s hands, allowing it to use the final months of its term to establish facts on the ground that will create a destructive reality which will be extremely difficult to reverse,” the NGOs said in a statement reacting to the ruling.

Three held after Karachi University professor assaulted at Safoora Chowrangi. KARACHI: Police on Tuesday arrested three suspects after a senior faculty member of the University of Karachi and his nephew were allegedly assaulted with pistol butts following a minor traffic accident near Safoora Chowrangi, police said. East Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Zubair Nazir Sheikh told Dawn that the victims were University of Karachi’s Islamic Learning Department chairman Dr Professor Mohammed Arif Khan Saqi and his nephew, Mohammed Waheed Rehman. “The professor was travelling along a main road on his way to the university, while the suspects were reversing their vehicle when it hit his,” SSP Sheikh said. He said the police had given the professor a letter for medico-legal formalities, following which a first information report (FIR) was registered at Sachal police station. “The police conducted raids and arrested three suspects. Further efforts were under way to arrest the remaining suspects,” he added. Sachal police station House Officer (SHO) Aijaz Pathan told Dawn that the suspects were influential persons who owned a restaurant in Safoora. He said raids were being conducted to arrest all those involved in the incident. Meanwhile, the FIR, registered on a complaint by Dr Saqi, invoked sections 147 (punishment for rioting), 148 (rioting while armed with a deadly weapon), 149 (every member of an unlawful assembly guilty of an offence committed in prosecution of the common object), 324 (attempt to commit qatl-i-amd) and 342 (punishment for wrongful confinement) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC). According to the complainant, he was travelling with his nephew in a car to the University of Karachi when the incident occurred. “When we reached Safoora Chowrangi near Green Hotel at around 10:15am, a double-cabin vehicle hit and damaged the bonnet of our car and attempted to drive away,” Dr Saqi said. He said the situation escalated when he asked the occupants of the vehicle to compensate for the damage to his car. Dr Saqi added that when he asked for their names, the suspects exited the vehicle and started assaulting his nephew. “In the meantime, their gunmen also arrived and started beating my nephew and me; as a result, we both fell on the road after being injured.” Later on, the suspects forcibly took them to a nearby eatery, the complainant said, adding that they were beaten again before the suspects fled.

Pakistan announces first national action plan to conserve sharks. Maritime Affairs Minister Muhammad Junaid Anwar Chaudhry on Tuesday announced the country’s first national action plan for shark conservation. The 10-year National Plan of Action for the Conservation and Management of Sharks (NPOA) will seek to restore declining shark populations, curb illegal finning and bycatch, protect critical marine habitats and promote sustainable fisheries in Pakistani waters through 2035. The plan is to be implemented in three phases, with an estimated $3.8 million to $5m in funding during its first five years. Chaudhry said the plan would be overseen by a multi-stakeholder National Advisory Committee. The minister said the plan sought to “strengthen fisheries management and enforcement while improving data collection and scientific research on shark populations”. Among the proposed measures are mandatory fins-naturally-attached policies, species-specific protections, shark sanctuaries, mangrove restoration and steps to reduce shark deaths as bycatch across fisheries. The plan also seeks to improve the livelihoods of coastal fishing communities through targeted support, while encouraging sustainable shark fisheries and greater international cooperation, including through Pakistan’s participation in the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission. Chaudhry said the implementation would be assessed annually against performance indicators such as landing-site monitoring coverage, completion of stock assessments, use of vessel monitoring systems and reductions in bycatch mortality. Formal reviews would be carried out every three years. The plan covers all chondrichthyan species found in Pakistani waters, including sharks, rays, skates and chimaeras, with a particular focus on species targeted by fisheries or facing high levels of bycatch mortality. “Although the primary emphasis is on sharks, the management frameworks, data collection systems and enforcement mechanisms established through the NPOA will also benefit other elasmobranch species,” the minister said. He said the action plan was tailored to Pakistan’s ecological, institutional and socio-economic conditions while remaining aligned with the Food and Agriculture Organisation’s International Plan of Action for Sharks and other international best practices. Chaudhry said preparation of the plan met Pakistan’s responsibilities as a shark-fishing nation under international fisheries law. The FAO’s international shark action plan encourages countries to develop national conservation and management plans, minimise waste and promote sustainable fishing practices, he added. “Responsible management of marine resources must come first,” Chaudhry said, stressing the need for stronger safeguards for vulnerable shark species and those whose capture is prohibited. According to a 2021 assessment by the World Wide Fund for Nature-Pakistan (WWF-P), shark landings in Pakistan decreased by over 85 per cent in five decades, which is more than the average decline in shark resources across the world. WWF-P had suggested a ban on the catch of endangered shark species and the import and export of shark fins at the time.

Sindh AG interrupts Mir Raza commission proceedings during police surgeon's testimony, objects to family's queries. KARACHI: A judicial commission formed to probe the circumstances and possible negligence around the Mir Raza Ali murder case issued notice to Sindh Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar after the Sindh Advocate General Jawad Dero interrupted the proceedings on Tuesday and objected to the lawyer representing the victims’ family asking any questions. The interruption came during Karachi Police Surgeon Dr Summaiya Syed’s testimony. The order issued after the commission’s proceedings stated: “It is regrettable that the commission’s proceedings have been interrupted by Sindh Advocate General Jawad Dero. He has objected to the family’s counsel asking any questions on behalf of the deceased’s family. “The highest law officer of the Sindh government making such a submission surprised me. It is more meaningful that the disturbance comes at a time when the police surgeon was explaining the role of senior police officers during the post-mortem examination.” The murder case has been mired in controversy, particularly after Dr Syed pointed out flaws in the findings of Ali’s first autopsy. Following that, Ali’s body was exhumed a second post-mortem was conducted. Dr Syed was part of the medical board that conducted the second autopsy, whose findings ruled out the possibility of suicide — a likelihood around which the law enforcers had initially tried to build the case. Meanwhile, Ali’s family accused police of trying to bury the facts. The one-member commission, headed by Sindh High Court Justice Omar Sial, heard the case today and noted in its order that Sindh Assembly member Faryal Talpur had suggested its formation to the provincial chief executive “for a transparent and impartial comprehensive investigation”. The order cited a Dawn report dated Aug 9, according to which, it said, Talpur stressed that justice for Ali must be ensured and “public should be transparently informed of all facts surrounding the case. The newspaper further cites her as saying that providing justice to the bereaved family and maintaining public confidence in the justice system was the fundamental responsibility of the government and relevant institutions”. Sindh Home Minister Lanjar and Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah had echoed these sentiments, the order stated. Justice Sial further wrote in the order that he was saddened that the advocate general had objected to requests by Ali’s family through their counsel for certain clarification. “It is the commission’s discretion to determine whether a query is relevant to the proceedings or not. Further, the commission’s terms of reference required it to find the true facts and circumstances of the case,” he said, adding that a notice was being issued to Lanjar to appear before the commission on Sept 10 and “put forward his stance […] as to whether the family is barred from asking questions to satisfy themselves that justice is being done”. Justice Sial further stated, “In my opinion, a deliberate attempt has been made by the Sindh advocate general to restrain the commission from addressing the family’s queries in a transparent manner.” Plea against FIR In a separate development, a two-member bench of the SHC, headed by Justice Muhammad Saleem Jessar and including Justice Abdul Hamid Bhurgri, took up a petition seeking the quashing of a case registered on August 27 against “around 100 people” for staging a protest in connection with the case. In the first information report (FIR), the protesters have been accused of blocking the road for vehicular movement and pedestrians at Karachi’s Sharea Faisal. The plea, a copy of which is available with Dawn , named Ammar Ahmed Khan, Muhammad Zubai Ali, Taha Shaikh, Zarar Khalid, Saad Shehriyar, and Hassan Surya as the petitioners. The SHC issued notices to the Sindh advocate general, the prosecutor general and other respondents for Nov 11 after hearing the plea today, directing that in the meantime, no coercive action should be taken against the petitioners. The court further directed that the investigation should be conducted strictly in accordance with the law and directed the petitioners to cooperate when required. “It is clarified that this order shall not be construed as an impediment in conducting the investigation strictly in accordance with law,” the court said. The case so far The body of 25-year-old Ali was found in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar last month, a day after he went missing on July 28. Days after the recovery of Ali’s body on July 29, Dr Syed had told Geo News that the post-mortem findings in the case had raised several questions, as some observations in the report did not appear to match the available photographs. On August 6, a Karachi court took up an application by Ali’s father, allowed the exhumation of his body, ordered the formation of a medico-legal board for the purpose and directed that a second autopsy of Ali’s body be conducted. The Sindh health department then constituted an eight-member board, with police surgeon Dr Syed as the convener. However, in the early hours of August 7, the board was reconstituted through an order issued by the director general of the Sindh health department. While Dr Syed remained the convener of the new five-member board, its members were changed. But Ali’s family rejected the new board, which also resulted in the deferment of the planned exhumation on Friday. Meanwhile, the counsel for Ali’s family, Nasir, accused the authorities of trying to bury the facts. The Sindh government then restored the original medical board, following which Ali’s body was exhumed on August 8. A day later, the Sindh inspector general of police’s (IG) office notified the reconstitution of the investigating team probing Ali’s death while Karachi Additional IG Azad Khan transferred the investigation into Ali’s murder to Zaman Town police station from Ferozabad Police Station, where the case was registered under charges of kidnapping. The order for the probe team’s reconstitution also showed that a murder charge had been added to the first information report. The same day, the Sindh government decided to seek a judicial commission for the case’s investigation, only to defer the plan a day later after Ali’s family said they had made no such demand and had faith in the new investigation team. On Aug 19, Ali’s parents, Mir Hussain and Mariam Hussain, wrote to Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, seeking his “direct supervision of the murder investigation”. They also urged the chief minister to order an investigation and departmental inquiry into the previous investigation team and immediately suspend the officers involved. The provincial government acknowledged the letter and announced the decision on Aug 23 to form a judicial commission to determine whether the investigation in the case was being conducted impartially and to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ali’s death. However, soon after the announcement, the counsel for Ali’s family raised objections and later approached the Sindh High Court (SHC). The petition was filed on August 24 in objection to the provincial government’s decision to form a judicial commission and sought the formation of an independent and multi-agency JIT “comprising officers who have had no previous involvement in the case” in place of the commission. On Sept 2, the SHC dismissed a petition filed by Ali’s family, seeking the formation of a JIT to probe his murder, observing that constituting such a body was the “prerogative of the government”. Meanwhile, the final report of Ali’s second post-mortem for the Mir Raza Ali murder case confirmed that his death was caused by a gunshot wound to the back. “Death occurred due to cardiac rupture consequent to perforating firearm injury of the chest,” the report stated, adding that the entry wound was on the posterior thorax (back) and the exit wound on the anterior thorax (front of the chest). “The findings are inconsistent with suicide as the manner of death,” it confirmed.

HRW cautions against normalising ties with Taliban amid rights concerns. WASHINGTON: Human Rights Watch (HRW) has warned countries against normalising engagement with the Taliban without clear and measurable human rights benchmarks, as a UN expert highlighted the devastating consequences of five years of Taliban rule for Afghan children and young people. “Countries should not normalise engagement with the Taliban without clear and measurable human rights benchmarks,” HRW said in a statement to the UN Human Rights Council on Monday. It urged states to recognise gender apartheid as a crime against humanity and support International Criminal Court (ICC) efforts to prosecute those responsible for gender persecution and other grave international crimes in Afghanistan. The warning came as Richard Bennett, the UN special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, issued a new report on the impact of Taliban policies on children. Bennett said the Taliban’s institutionalised system of discrimination, repression and ideological control was depriving children of their rights to inclusive and quality education, freedom of expression and meaningful participation in social and public life. “Afghanistan’s children are growing up in an environment where discrimination, especially against girls and women, is being normalised; they are denied the right to learn and their opportunities for the future are dramatically shrinking,” Bennett said. He expressed particular concern over the continued denial of education beyond the sixth grade to girls and the growing exposure of children and young people to gender-based violence, forced and child marriage, child labour and ideological indoctrination. “These policies are not only violating children’s rights today — they are undermining their ability to determine their own futures,” Bennett said. “For girls in particular, the systematic denial of education is closing doors that may never reopen, with serious consequences for their mental health and the country’s development as a whole.” The report said these abuses were taking place against a backdrop of decades of conflict, poverty and unmet humanitarian needs. By dismantling or weakening institutions that previously protected children’s rights, the Taliban had exposed Afghan children to greater risks of violence, abuse and exploitation, Bennett said. Children living in poverty or remote areas, those with disabilities, members of marginalised religious and ethnic communities, and displaced children or those returning from abroad are among the most vulnerable, he said. Bennett also warned that restrictions on media, culture and freedom of expression were limiting the diversity of ideas and experiences available to Afghan children. “Children need space to learn, to think freely, to express themselves and imagine a different future,” he said. “Instead, many are growing up in fear, isolation and uncertainty.” The restrictions, combined with limited educational opportunities, were contributing to a growing sense of despair and could create future security concerns and a migration crisis, Bennett warned. He cautioned, however, against viewing Afghan children only as victims, noting their resilience and determination to support their families and communities and pursue alternative forms of learning. Bennett urged the Taliban to end discriminatory policies, restore comprehensive education for girls, strengthen child protection and justice systems, prevent child and forced marriage and child labour, prohibit corporal punishment, and restore inclusive healthcare and social protection for children with disabilities. He also called on other countries to fully fund humanitarian assistance, expand alternative education for girls and safe pathways for Afghans at risk, and support mine-action programmes, youth initiatives and international accountability efforts. “Five years of restrictive rule and socio-economic collapse have fundamentally altered the conditions in which Afghanistan’s children are growing up,” Bennett said. “The international community must act now to protect their rights and ensure that present and future generations are not deprived of the opportunity to shape Afghanistan’s future.” HRW, meanwhile, said gender persecution had become further entrenched over the past year, with the Taliban dismantling already limited legal protections for women and girls. “Since 2021, Taliban authorities have systematically deprived women and girls of their fundamental rights,” the organisation said. HRW cited a new criminal procedure code that recognises only “excessive” beating as domestic violence against women, potentially leaving survivors of other forms of abuse without effective avenues for justice. It also said a decree concerning judicial separation had eliminated minimum-age protections for girls’ marriage. Journalists, human rights defenders, peaceful protesters and former government employees continue to face arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, torture and other serious abuses, HRW said. The organisation urged UN member states to renew Bennett’s mandate and provide his office with the resources needed to independently monitor and report on Afghanistan. It also called for the urgent operationalisation of the Human Rights Council’s new independent accountability mechanism for the country. HRW further urged governments not to forcibly return people to Afghanistan, where persecution remains systematic and well documented, and to support efforts by the International Criminal Court to prosecute those responsible for gender persecution and other grave international crimes. “Afghan victims, survivors and their families have waited far too long for truth, justice, and reparation,” HRW said. Separately, UN Secretary-General António Guterres renewed his call on the Taliban to lift restrictions preventing Afghan women working for the UN from entering its premises and carrying out their duties. The UN has said the restrictions hamper its ability to deliver assistance and services to the Afghan population, particularly women and girls. The warnings from Bennett, HRW and Guterres come as the Taliban regime approaches five years in power, with the UN expert warning that its policies are affecting not only the rights of Afghans today but the prospects of an entire generation of children.

PMDC instructs medical, dental colleges not to admit Afghan students for 'current academic session'. ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) has barred medical and dental colleges from granting admission or placement to Afghan students for the current academic session, and students previously enrolled in such programmes are “required to return to Afghanistan”, Dawn has learnt. The policy decision was conveyed by the council to public and private medical institutions across the country earlier this month. The PMDC communique, seen by Dawn , dated Sept 1, 2026, calls on all institutions to ensure the completion of administrative formalities to facilitate the departure of Afghan students. “It is further reiterated that Afghan nationals previously enrolled in medical or dental programs in Pakistan are required to return to Afghanistan, in accordance with the prevailing policy directions,” said the PMDC communique. “The concerned institutions shall ensure that all necessary administrative formalities, including issuance of requisite NOCs and facilitation of their departure are completed, accordingly,” added the council. The development came amid reports, circulating on social media, about the alleged expulsion of Afghan nationals who were studying at public sector medical colleges in Lahore. According to a health ministry official, an “in principle” decision had been made to send Afghan students enrolled in Pakistani medical universities back to their country, due to the ongoing tensions between Islamabad and Kabul. “Letters have been written to all medical universities asking their constituent colleges about the number of Afghan nationals enrolled in medical and dental colleges. Universities have also been directed to provide details of how many students are studying in each year,” he explained. The official said the PMDC had details of most Afghan medical students; however, “there remained a possibility that some may have been missed or mistakenly identified as nationals of other countries or as locals”. “After getting the information, lists will be shared with the concerned quarters, and the rest will be decided by them,” he said. However, he also clarified that the decision did not apply to students of other nationalities, only Afghan students. When asked about the reported expulsion of Afghan students, Foreign Office (FO) spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told Dawn : “As per the Illegal Foreigner Repatriation Plan (IFRP), stay of any foreign national without a valid visa and passport is illegal, and the concerned individual is liable to deportation.” Khan added that Pakistani authorities were continuing to process visa extension applications from Afghan students “in line with our existing policy, rules and regulations”. The vice chancellor of a medical university confirmed receipt of the PMDC instructions, saying that institutions had begun collecting Afghan students’ particulars in line with the council’s instructions. “There were a number of students enrolled in undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. Although we were directed to provide the data, we were not told why such action was being taken,” he said. Millions of Afghans have poured into Pakistan over the past several decades, fleeing successive wars, including hundreds of thousands who arrived after the Taliban returned to power in 2021. In June, the Ministry of Interior issued a directive to immediately arrest any Afghan national “found residing in Pakistan without a valid visa” from July 10. A deportation drive first launched in 2023 was renewed in April last year when the government rescinded hun­dreds of thousands of residence permits for Afghans, warning them of arrests if they did not leave. Last year alone, over a million Afghan nationals were deported by Pakistan, a Senate Standing Committee on Kashmir Affairs, Gilgit-Baltistan and States and Frontier Regions (SAFRON) was informed. Pakistan deported a total of 1,155,221 Afghan nationals in 2025, top officials of the Ministry of Interior and Chief Commissionerate for Afghan Refugees told the meeting. The repatriation push also comes as relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan have deteriorated. Pakistan has repeatedly urged the Afghan Taliban government to rein in terrorist hideouts in Afghanistan and prevent militant groups from carrying out attacks against Pakistan from Afghan soil. However, its appeals have gone unheeded.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs364.35 per litre while HSD will cost Rs385.95 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable on Sept 9 (Wednesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Exchange companies’ dollar sales jump 30pc. KARACHI: Exchange companies’ dollar sales to banks increased by 30 per cent year-on-year in August, indicating higher inflows. Data from the Exchange Companies Association of Pakistan (ECAP) showed these companies sold $248.7 million to banks in August, up from $174.9m in the same month last year. However, July saw a decline to $230.7m, down from $290.6m in the corresponding month last year. Pakistan has remained unaffected by the Gulf war as far as remittances are concerned, but reports in the media that Pakistani workers are being sent back home from Gulf countries have caused fear. ECAP reports $248.7m sold to banks in August The government has also noted the situation, while the market fears a shock if the war continues to drag on in the region. Pakistan is already struggling to manage high oil prices , the main victim of the war. The August inflow could be higher if the disturbance in Kashmir were fully controlled. However, Malik Bostan, Chairman ECAP, said the situation has begun to normalise in Kashmir and inflows have increased. “There could have been $50m more inflows during July-Aug this year had the Kashmir situation not been disrupted by political conflicts,” said Malik Bostan. He said the ECAP has officially requested the State Bank to allow internet access across the entire Kashmir, while partial internet access has already been restored. The exchange companies collectively sold $479.5m in 2MFY27, up from $465.5m in 2MFY26. Pakistan expects higher remittances in FY27, with the target set at $44 billion against an inflow of $41.5bn in FY26. However, currency experts said the prolonged war has changed the economic situation across the Middle East. Gulf countries are desperate because they cannot sell their only income-generating product, oil. “The UAE was the most thriving economy in the region, but the situation has changed its economy; now the country is trying hard not to expel expatriates, which may paint a bleak picture of Dubai,” said a currency expert. Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026

Public Accounts Committee flags Rs22.8m drug shortage at Quetta hospital. • Raises concern over irregularities in medicine purchases at Sandeman Provincial Civil Hospital • Hospital and health officials failed to produce complete records; committee gives health dept 15 days to submit records QUETTA: The Balochistan Asse­mbly’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has expressed serious concern over alleged irregularities in the purchase of medicines worth millions of rupees and the reported disappearance of drugs worth Rs22.825 million from the central store of Sandeman Provincial Civil Hospital, Quetta. The committee directed the health department and hospital administration to submit all relevant records, explanations and supporting documents within 15 days, warning that failure to provide satisfactory explanations could lead to recommendations for referring the matter to the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) or registration of an FIR. The PAC meeting was chaired by its chairman, Asghar Ali Tareen, and attended by committee members. The meeting reviewed in detail audit paragraphs from the special audit of Sandeman Provincial Civil Hospital for 2022-23. The committee was informed that Rs10.443 billion had been allocated or provided to the hospital between the financial years 2017-18 and 2021-22, of which Rs9.576 billion had been spent. However, the health department and hospital authorities had failed to provide complete expenditure accounts and the required record. PAC members expressed strong displeasure over the department’s failure to provide the required documents on time and its alleged non-compliance with previous PAC directives. Mr Tareen said the health department had been presenting only its own position before the committee for the past one-and-a-half years, while rules and regulations were not being properly implemented. He said this created the impression that the department was not taking the assembly and PAC seriously. The committee also examined an audit paragraph concerning the purchase of medicines worth Rs30.016 million. According to the special audit, significant irregularities had been found in the procurement process. The audit report stated that the supply order was issued to M/s FDL, Peshawar, while payment was made to M/s Health Tech, Quetta. The audit also pointed out discrepancies between supply orders and bills, missing entries in the stock register, and the absence of delivery challans and inspection reports. The department later told the Departmental Accounts Committee (DAC) that FDL was the manufacturing agency and Health Tech was its authorised distributor. However, during verification, several requi­red documents, including FDL’s consent, stock register, delivery challans, inspection reports, medicine batch details and other relevant records, were not produced. The PAC chairman directed the authorities to complete and submit all relevant records within 15 days. The committee also reviewed an audit paragraph concerning medicines worth Rs22.825 million reportedly missing from the hospital’s central store during 2019-20. Under GFR 151, Volume I, the store officer was responsible for the safe custody, proper record-keeping and accounting of government stores to prevent theft, damage or fraud. The special audit found that medicines worth Rs22.825 million were missing from the central store. Although the pharmacist in charge had brought the matter to the administration’s attention, it remained unresolved. Delivery challans and inspection committee reports were also unavailable in the official record. The department denied any shortage, but record scrutiny revealed discrepancies in stock balances, for which no satisfactory explanation was provided. Mr Tareen said merely suspending employees was not a solution. He said the chief secretary would be informed of the situation in writing and that the report and the matter would also be presented before the Balochistan Assembly. At the conclusion of the meeting, the health department was directed to submit within 15 days all records, explanations and documents relating to the two audit paragraphs for consideration by the PAC. Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026

Protest politics. WITH the PTI determined to march on the capital on Sept 27, a l egal challenge to the planned protest has been lodged in the Islamabad High Court. The petitioner — ostensibly an Islamabad trader — fears disruption of routine life and business activities because of the protest. While hearing the petition on Tuesday, the IHC formed a larger bench to hear the “sensitive” case, with the next hearing scheduled for tomorrow. Clearly, there is unease within the corridors of power regarding the PTI’s planned power show, which the party says is being organised for the “supremacy of the Constitution” and to demand the release of its founder Imran Khan. The government’s concern was on full display in Karachi on Sunday , when large parts of the city’s road network were shut down on the day KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi was due to hold a rally at the Quaid’s mausoleum. Though the Sindh authorities claimed the shutdowns had nothing to do with the PTI’s planned activities and were carried out due to ‘security’ reasons, major thoroughfares had been blocked off on the day Mr Khan’s party was to stage its rally in the city. The state believes that letting the PTI go ahead with the Islamabad rally could result in violence. These apprehensions are not without basis. After all, the November 2024 protest in the capital resulted in a deadly showdown between the party and the state. Yet there are two distinct issues that must be kept in mind. Firstly, holding a protest is a democratic right, and the authorities should not be placing unnecessary obstacles in the PTI’s way. If the government blocks every democratic avenue to express grievances, it risks radicalising the affected parties. Secondly, though protest is a fundamental right, it must not turn violent. Attacks on law enforcers and harassment of ordinary citizens are unacceptable, and it is the responsibility of party leaders to ensure that their cadres remain non-violent. It is not just the PTI that has sought to highlight its grievances on the streets; the Jamaat-i-Islami has been holding nationwide sit-ins over fuel prices for several weeks. While one may or may not agree with the reasons why these parties have hit the streets, their right to hold peaceful protest is undeniable. When there are so many challenges confronting the people — high prices, economic volatility, terrorism, political uncertainty, erosion of democratic space, etc. — they cannot be expected to keep quiet, and have every right to voice their concerns publicly. The state should engage the PTI just as it engaged the JI to ensure that any protest is kept peaceful. The animosity should not be allowed to snowball into a fresh confrontation as the nation can ill afford more instability. Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026
