Religious freedom subject to law, policy and morality: Federal Constitu­tional Court. • Court upholds ban on 23-volume Ahmadi publication • Ruling notes ban was based on Ulema board’s decision, merely conveyed by chief secretary’s office ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitu­tional Court (FCC) on Tuesday affirmed that fundamental rights, including the right to religious freedom, are not absolute but must be balanced against broader public considerations. The observation came while dismissing a series of petitions challenging the government’s ban on a 23-volume Ahmadiyya publication. Headed by Justice Aamer Farooq, a two-judge bench, also comprising Justice Syed Arshad Hussain Shah, delivered the consolidated judgement, rejecting petitions filed by Muhammad Abdul Qadoos and several others against notifications issued by the Punjab government under Section 99-A of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) and Section 19 of the Press, Newspapers, News Agencies and Books Registration Ordinance, 2002. The petitioners had challenged the Oct 13, 2025, and April 30, 2024, judgements of the Lahore High Court, as well as its Multan bench, which had dismissed their petitions on the grounds of laches and their failure to avail themselves of an alternate remedy within the prescribed limitation period. In their appeal before the FCC, the petitioners challenged the legality of Notification No. SO (IS-III) 6-15/2010, issued by the Punjab Home Department on June 25, 2014, under Section 99-A of the CrPC. Through the notification, Rohani Khazayeen, Volumes 1 to 23 was banned and all its copies ordered to be forfeited. The petitioners also contended that the executive action banning the publications had infringed upon their right to religious freedom guaranteed under Article 20 of the Constitution. Authored by Justice Farooq, the 13-page judgement explained that Article 20 guarantees religious freedom subject to law, public policy and morality. It also rebuffed the petitioners’ claim that Article 20 had been violated, observing that determining the validity of the ban and forfeiture required careful examination of the strength and underlying reasoning of the action taken under the CrPC and relevant ordinance. The judgement said the court could not proceed on mere assumptions, particularly in the absence of the actual material on record due to the petitioners’ failure to avail themselves of the appropriate remedies. “It is restated that the assertion of the counsel for the petitioners that the impugned actions on part of the executive violate their Religious Freedom clause seems to be an afterthought and was nothing more than wittering on about the subject of Fundamental Rights in general and Religious Freedom clause in particular,” the judgement observed. It added that instead of attempting to show the court the content of the material and its impact, the petitioners’ counsel had made a general discourse. The judgement highlighted that under the Punjab Rules of Business, 2011, authority had been duly delegated to the provincial government and, since the home department was responsible for taking action in such matters, it had acted competently. Regarding the allegation that the publications had been forfeited without application of mind, the judgement explained that, according to the record, an Ulema board had been constituted which, after deliberations, decided that the material in the volumes could cause hatred among the Muslim community and recommended that it be forfeited. The judgement said the impugned forfeiture action emanated from the office of the Chief Secretary. However, the determinative inquiry was not the identity of the functionary but the legal source of the power exercised. In the present case, the authority was clearly traceable to statutory instruments, namely the CrPC and the ordinance. These enactments expressly empowered the chief secretary to undertake the measure taken, thereby placing the action within a statutorily conferred framework rather than the realm of unfettered executive discretion, the judgement explained. In conclusion, the FCC dismissed all petitions, refused leave to appeal and disposed of all pending applications. Published in Dawn, September 9th, 2026

Pitfalls of referendum. THE plot thickens. What the ubiquitous interior minister said makes at least one thing clear: restructuring the existing administrative framework is inevitable. It was apparent that he was not voicing the view of the civilian dispensation but that of the powers that be. “New administrative units will have to be created. No one can stop it,” he declared. There was also a clear hint that a referendum might be held to determine the “will of the people” on the issue. Mohsin Naqvi, a man of all seasons, appears to have been handed yet another political project — added to a portfolio that already ranges from overseeing internal security to running cricket affairs and occasional diplomatic troubleshooting. What makes him so powerful is that he answers to neither the prime minister nor parliament. His new assignment, however, looks exceptionally challenging. The proposed ‘administrative restructuring’ plan — its contours still unclear — has generated a political maelstrom that threatens the existing political order. It has not only divided the federal cabinet but also ruptured the ruling alliance . The PPP has already launched a campaign against any attempt to divide Sindh under the pretext of administrative restructuring. A strongly worded resolution against the plan, passed by the Sindh Assembly last week, offers some insight into the volatility of the situation in the country’s second-largest province. The brewing conflict between the province and the federal government has now exploded, threatening to bring down the present political set-up. The rupture is hard to mend. More intriguing, however, is the response of the prime minister and the ruling PML-N on the proposed administrative restructuring — said to be floated by the establishment. While there is no word from the PM , the differing voices from the PML-N and other cabinet ministers on the proposed plan presented by the interior minister make the entire issue extremely complicated. It is a house divided on a proposed plan whose framework remains obscure. No move to restructure governance should be separated from the democratic process. There seems to be complete confusion in the ranks of the ruling party. While some PML-N cabinet members and party officials appear supportive of the administrative restructuring, the party’s top leadership has maintained a conspicuous silence over the proposed plan. A big question also hangs over whether the PML-N leadership is prepared to support a plan to divide Punjab — its main power base. Matters are getting murkier, with the establishment appearing adamant to go ahead with its plan with or without political support, as Naqvi has warned. With its governments in Islamabad and Lahore fully dependent on the establishment’s support for survival, the PML-N has no choice but to toe the line. As for the PTI — the main opposition party, arguably the most popular in the country, which also governs the troubled province of KP — it may not oppose administrative restructuring on principle, but it will not support any imposed plan . With its mandate stolen and its leaders imprisoned, one cannot expect the party to accept any proposal that would strengthen the establishment’s control. In this scenario, it will be extremely hard for the establishment to push through a plan requiring a two-thirds majority in both parliament and the provincial assemblies, as the Constitution demands. Even a constitutional amendment would need a two-thirds majority in both Houses, and with the PPP refusing to come on board, things could get messier. Yet it seems the powers that be are not willing to back down. Their only choice, then, would be to go for a referendum, as Naqvi has hinted. With the PML-N and other coalition partners on board, it may not be difficult to get a referendum resolution passed by parliament with a simple majority. Pakistan has a history of referendums being used by military dictators in an attempt to legitimise their unconstitutional rule. Who can forget the infamous referendum held by Gen Ziaul Haq to perpetuate his illegitimate government? Interestingly, the question was not whether Zia should stay as president, but whether voters would like an Islamic system to be established — a ‘yes’ vote was to count as validation of Ziaul Haq as president. Ballot boxes were stuffed to cover up the thin turnout, and the mockery further exposed the illegitimacy of military rule. Gen Pervez Musharraf held a similar referendum to legitimise his rule, though there it directly asked voters to approve his presidency. While turnout remained low, the official statement declared massive support for the military ruler. Will the present dispensation resort to the same kind of fraudulent exercise to carry out its so-called restructuring plan? There is also a strong apprehension that a referendum could be used to enshrine a constitutional role for the security establishment in the power structure — a recent bill passed by parliament has only reinforced that speculation. There are no two views that the country needs major restructuring to improve governance, but it cannot be separated from the democratic process. In a situation where the legitimacy of the entire system is questionable, no measure, however feasible it may sound, can be acceptable. Indeed, devolution to the lower tier of local government is essential if the system is to deliver, but in the absence of democracy, any administrative restructuring would likely strengthen authoritarian rule. No referendum can confer legitimacy on an imposed administrative structure. The proposal, though still unclear, has already polarised the country, and any referendum will only intensify chaos and instability. The best thing for the country is to hold free and fair elections and let an elected parliament decide on the critical issues of administrative restructuring and devolution of power to local governments. The present establishment-backed rule, with its questionable mandate, cannot be expected to bring democracy to the grassroots. The lessons of the past must not be forgotten — of authoritarian regimes that tried to strengthen their control in the name of reform. A reminder to the interior minister who referred to Zohran Mamdani and Sadiq Khan: the two mayors are the products of democracy, and no leader like them can emerge under semi-authoritarian rule. Hidden barriers. PAKISTAN is the fifth most populous country in the world. Nearly seven million babies are born in Pakistan each year — approximately 19,000 every day. The urgency of family planning is difficult to exaggerate. Yet the scale of the crisis can tempt us into believing that the solution is simple: create awareness, provide contraceptives and persuade couples to have fewer children. The reality in Pakistan is far more complicated. When my organisation began facilitating family planning services in villages in Larkana district, we initially referred women to a government reproductive health services centre in Larkana city. There, they could receive contraceptives or undergo tubal ligation, a permanent method commonly described as having one’s ‘tubes tied’. The services were free. At one stage, women were even offered a few hundred rupees as an incentive to undergo tubal ligation. On paper, the system appeared accessible. In practice, getting through it could become a test of endurance. A woman would travel from her village to Larkana, only to be told that she first needed a medical test. She would have it done and return a week later. This time, she might be told that the doctor was absent and she should come again. On her next visit, there could be another administrative or medical impediment. For a middle-class urban patient, a postponed appointment is an inconvenience. For a poor rural woman, it may end the process altogether. Every visit requires transport money, permission or cooperation from her family, arrangements for the children left at home and the sacrifice of an entire working day. She may need someone to accompany her. If she or her husband is a daily-wage worker, the household also loses income. Family planning programmes must be designed around the woman’s complete journey. We then changed our approach. Instead of referring women and expecting them to negotiate the system themselves, we began taking them through the process. Our team picks up the woman from her village in our vehicle and takes her to the facility. We handle documentation and consultation so that the procedure appears less daunting and is completed that day. We also provide nutritional support and take her back home. A team member visits the following day to check on her recovery and ensure that she receives the pain relief, antibiotics or other medicines prescribed by the doctor. Further visits are made for wound care and the removal of sutures. This is what access actually looks like in a rural setting. The procedure may be free, but reaching it is not. Someone must bridge the distance between the village and the hospital, help the woman navigate the institution and remain responsible for her aftercare. We were once told that the Population Welfare Department had vehicles available to transport women. Yet that arrangement never worked reliably for our patients. We were told the vehicle has been deployed elsewhere, needs repair or will only come if several women meet at one location. A vehicle listed in a departmental inventory is meaningless if a woman cannot depend upon it on the day she needs it. Transport and bureaucracy, however, are only part of the difficulty. The deeper barriers are social. We encountered cases in which doctors refused to perform tubal ligations on women who had no sons, only one son, or a son younger than 10. When questioned, the doctors described cases in which a woman underwent sterilisation and later lost her only son to illness or an accident. Her family then expected her to produce another boy. If she could no longer conceive, her husband might marry again, diminishing her status and security within the household. Some women later returned, desperate to have the sterilisation reversed. Reversal is complex, expensive, available only at specialised centres and does not guarantee that fertility will be restored. These concerns reveal the cruel consequences of son preference and women’s dependence within marriage. But they also raise a difficult question: should a doctor protect a woman from a possible future injustice by denying her control over her body today? Surely, the answer cannot be a blanket refusal based on the number or ages of her sons. The appropriate response is careful, private and informed counselling. A woman should understand that tubal ligation is intended to be permanent. She should also receive information about long-acting reversible methods. Community health workers and doctors must ensure that her decision is voluntary and free from pressure. Once an adult woman understands the implications and gives informed consent, her reproductive choice should not depend upon whether she has produced a son. Modern contraceptive use among married Pakistani women remains low, while around one in six has an unmet need for family planning. Distance, cost, unreliable services, the need for permission or accompaniment and limited decision-making power all reduce contraceptive uptake. We will not overcome these barriers through awareness campaigns alone. Family planning programmes must be designed around the woman’s complete journey. Who will counsel her in terms she understands? Who will take her to the hospital? Who will ensure that the doctor is present, the tests are completed and her chosen method is available? Who will bring her home and respond if she develops a complication? Unless these questions have reliable answers, we do not have a functioning family planning programme. We have services on paper and women stranded many miles away from them. Pakistan’s population challenge is urgent. But urgency must not produce coercion or an assembly-line approach to women’s bodies. The last mile of family planning is covered only when a woman can make an informed choice, reach dependable care and return home safely. Until we build that bridge, we should not be surprised when women fail to cross it. Federal Constitutional Court moved for ban on social media use by kids under 16. LAHORE: A petition has been filed before the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), seeking directions to shield children under 16 from unrestricted social media use and indecent content on television and other platforms. Two lawyers, Sheraz Zaka and Moin Akhtar, filed the petition at the Lahore registry, with the former identifying himself as an activist and the latter as the father of a minor child. The petitioners argue that Pakistani children are being exposed to cyber bullying, addictive platform design, sexualised content and the glorification of alcohol — all of which they say harm children’s mental and moral development. They claim that no Pakistani law currently mandates age verification for social media access, noting that the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca), 2016, contains no specific restriction for users under 16. Citing examples of Australia, Italy, and Brazil as countries that have already imposed under-16 social media bans , the petitioners argue that such regulation is both feasible and necessary. Plea claims no law mandates age verification for social media access They allege that the Pemra failed to enforce its own code of conduct, allowing dramas and advertisements containing intimate scenes and alcohol depictions to air during hours when children are likely watching. The petitioners also refer to Pakistan’s broader education crisis, citing figures that roughly 25 million children in the country are out of school — reportedly the highest number of out-of-school children anywhere in the world. The petitioners assert that the government’s failure to act violates articles 9, 14, 25, 25-A and 35 of the Constitution, which guard the rights to life, dignity, equality, education and family protection. They also invoke the Convention on the Rights of the Child and a prior Lahore High Court ruling (PLD 2020 Lahore 137) that directed the state to legislate on human rights and social issues. The lawyers ask the FFC to direct the federal government to amend Peca 2016 to restrict social media access for under-16s with an age-verification mechanism, and and order to the Pemra to strictly enforce content standards during child-viewing hours. They also seek a direction to the government for coordination with social media platforms on parental controls and action on out-of-school children and dropout rates. The petitioners describe it as the first such petition filed in the country on the issue. The federal government through the ministry of law and justice, the ministry of information technology, the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency, the Pemra and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority have been listed as respondents in the petition. Iran attacks American base in Jordan, ships near Hormuz after US hits oil tankers. Iran’s Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) said it fired ballistic missiles at a base in Jordan used by the US military and attacked 10 ships on Wednesday, after the US said it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers, in a sharp escalation of the six-month-old war. Increased attacks by both the US and Iran have shattered a month of relative calm, hitting military, shipping and energy assets, sending oil prices surging and drawing in regional allies in recent days. The US military’s Central Command posted video of the strikes, which it called a response to IRGC targeting a US Navy warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the US said. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia. Iran then carried out a ballistic missile attack on a base used by US forces near Al Azraq in Jordan, according to an IRGC statement on state media. Although Iran said its missiles inflicted heavy damage, Jordan said its air defences intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling in unpopulated areas, and that there were no casualties. A US official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for. The IRGC said on Wednesday it also attacked 10 ships, including two US Vessels and eight oil tankers, attempting to cross a “prohibited and unsafe” area of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit largely choked off by Iranian attacks. Iran has targeted US assets and allies in the region throughout the war, including in Jordan several times, killing at least two US military personnel during one strike in July. Iran has also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement carried by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan, though it was unclear who was responsible. Oil prices extended gains in early trade on Wednesday with Brent crude nearing $100 a barrel on market concerns over the disruption of oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Recent attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on top energy producer Saudi Arabia have added to supply concerns. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia On Tuesday, Houthis launched an attack on several cities in Saudi Arabia, further undermining regional stability. The Houthi attacks wounded 73 people and set oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a major expansion of the conflict, which began on February 28 with joint US-Israeli attacks on Iran. The Houthis, who control most of Yemen’s populated areas, including the capital, have further pressured US allies by periodically disrupting shipping on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, at the entrance to the Red Sea. They said they had launched a broad operation deep into Saudi territory, using drones and missiles to strike a Saudi air base in the southern city of Khamis Mushait as well as Saudi state oil company assets in the cities of Abha, Najran and Jazan. Saudi authorities reported blazes at the sites and said women and children were among the wounded. The wider war in the Gulf has turned into a test of wills between the US and Iran, with each side hoping that economic pressure from competing blockades will force the other to yield. Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz, while cutting off Iran’s exports with a blockade. Central Command said the tankers it destroyed on Tuesday were part of a shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies.

Anthropic researcher resigns, says AI labs are ‘gambling with our lives’. A researcher at Anthropic has tendered his resignation, warning that artificial intelligence (AI) labs are racing to develop systems that could pose a “threat” to human life within years. Jacob Coxon’s departure was first reported by the Wall Street Journal , which said it was “one of the first examples of an Anthropic employee leaving over AI safety fears”. In a thread on the social media platform X, Coxon — a researcher who specialises in training new AI models by having them consume vast amounts of data — said: “I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pre-training research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he added. “Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he said. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing,” he added. Coxon also warned of fears among AI researchers and executives about the potential consequences of the technology. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible — but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger,” he said. Coxon questioned why companies continued developing AI despite such concerns. “A common response is ‘if they truly believe this, why are they still building it?’ At OpenAI, many have not deeply internalised the civilisational stakes,” he said. “At Anthropic, the stakes are well-understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first — they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk,” he added. Coxon urged AI researchers to reconsider the pace of development and the risks involved, saying: “If you are a lab researcher, I urge you to consider what the next few years will actually feel like. “Do you want to kick off a superintelligent RL run without a rigorous understanding of its mind? Should you put your head down because ‘it’s happening anyway’ — or take this moment to call for different conditions?” he asked. Speaking to the Journal , Coxon had voiced the same reasons for his departure, saying he did not want to participate in an industrywide rush to “build AI systems that can improve themselves, worried such systems could spiral out of control and destroy humanity”. He also said that many of his industry colleagues now used phrases like “crunchtime” and “endgame” to describe the trajectory toward self-improving models. The report said that he was also among more than 1,000 AI researchers who recently signed a statement urging global government coordination on a system to “slow AI development if a brake pedal is needed to control models capable of improving on their own”.

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday escalated his trade war against Canada, banning imports of alcohol and various products and raising tariffs on others, with the conflict showing no sign of abating. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney stood firm, acknowledging that reducing economic ties with the United States would come at a cost but saying the benefits would outweigh the pain. A range of Canadian products, from mattresses to motorboats and golf carts, will be subject to a 50 per cent surcharge beginning September 15, according to Trump’s executive order issued late on Tuesday. The import ban, which targets various alcoholic beverages as well as some dairy products like whey, will come into effect on September 29, according to other executive orders issued at the same time. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect earlier on Tuesday, applying to $20 billion in US imports, including steel and aluminium products and dairy goods such as cheese, in response to duties announced by Washington on August 22. Canada has “everything we need to pivot and prosper”, Carney said in a video address. “That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still.” ‘Discriminatory treatment’ Responding to the latest Canadian levies, Trump pledged to restrict Canadian companies from securing US government contracts. In a social media post earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was directing officials “to remove Canadian-origin products from GSA’s Multiple Award Schedules,” referring to a General Services Administration program for long-term contracts. — Screengrab via Truth Social Contracts through such schedules account for more than $50 billion a year, Trump added. On Monday, Trump threatened to try to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the United States. In response, the aerospace company pointed to its creation of tens of thousands of jobs across the United States, with direct employment in more than 20 states, including Kansas, Texas, Arizona, and California. The two Republican senators representing Kansas said they had conveyed their concerns to the White House. “I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s more than 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Senator Roger Marshall posted on X, with similar comments posted by Senator Jerry Moran. US tariffs pose a modestly negative risk to Canada’s overall economy, but analysts note that they have a sharper impact on central Canada’s manufacturing sector. ‘Lake America’ “I don’t believe in escalating the conflict. That’s not constructive,” Carney said in his video statement on Tuesday. “But our tariffs are necessary to protect our workers, protect our companies, and protect our communities. “This is about who we are as Canadians.” Reacting to Trump’s move, Canada’s minister in charge of trade with the United States, Dominic LeBlanc, said late on Tuesday that Ottawa was “assessing the latest tariff measures”. Negotiations between the two sides broke down on August 21 after days of meetings in Washington. At the time, Carney said US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the eleventh hour, as well as unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”. Ottawa and Washington have not resumed talks since. On Sunday, Trump posted an illustration of himself towering over Carney as they played ice hockey, with Trump saying, “Get up, governor,” a reference to his determination to turn Canada into another US state. Trump also signed an order in August to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as “Lake America,” sparking fury in Canada amid a broader wave of patriotism triggered by the US president’s hostility. Although Carney is backed by Canadian public opinion, his country remains reliant on its neighbour. Nearly 60pc of Canada’s imports come from the United States, and about 70pc of its exports go to the US market. To help businesses and workers, Canada’s government has unveiled an aid package worth $5.4bn.

'Instead of speaking at business forums, Naqvi should visit Parliament': Bilawal on interior minister's call for governance rest. Amid growing debate in the country on the creation of new provinces to improve governance, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari has said that the issue should be debated in Parliament. He expressed these views while speaking to the media in London, where he is on a visit with his father, President Asif Ali Zardari. During the trip, President Zardari held a meeting with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who in July sparked a political maelstrom by calling for an overhaul of the country’s governance structure and the creation of new provinces. During the media interaction in London, Bilawal was asked about the matter and questioned about “whose language Mohsin Naqvi sahib was speaking”. “Mohsin Naqvi sahib must be speaking his own language, and I speak my language. It is his right to express his opinion,” Bilawal said. He said that the creation of new provinces should be debated in the National Assembly, adding that, however, Naqvi rarely visited the lower house of Parliament. “So instead of [speaking at] business forums, Mohsin Naqvi should visit [Parliament],” he remarked, an apparent reference to the first instance of Naqvi stressing the need for more administrative units while speaking at the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in July. Bilawal reiterated that the matter should be debated in Parliament. “I am ready to debate this with any representative of the federal government or a federal minister,” he said. He added that problems and faults that had “historically” existed in the system should be openly discussed. “The real issues resulting in the system’s collapse and their solutions should be discussed in Parliament by the people’s elected representatives,” Bilawal stressed. The proposal by Naqvi in July drew strong reactions from government ministers, while the country’s leading lawyers’ bodies adopted divergent positions . However, the PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre, has strongly opposed the move. It has also maintained that any decision to create new provinces must be taken through the constitutional and parliamentary process and with political consensus. Its opposition is mainly to the proposed division of Sindh, but the party has long advocated for a South Punjab province , and so has the opposition PTI. On the other hand, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) — which is an ally of the Centre coalition but forms the opposition in Sindh — has been demanding that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh. President Zardari’s meeting with Naqvi in London was followed by the Sindh Assembly adopting a resolution rejecting all attempts to divide the province or create new administrative units. Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah declared that “there will be no compromise on Sindh’s geographical unity”. On Tuesday, the Sindh Assembly Secretariat also sent letters to the principal secretaries to the president and prime minister, and to the Senate and National Assembly, informing them about the resolution. Meanwhile, two days after the resolution was passed, Naqvi doubled down on his demand for new provinces. “New administrative units will eventually have to be created as Pakistan’s growing population and changing needs can no longer be effectively managed through the existing administrative structure,” said the minister, who is considered close to the powers that be. Addressing a National Policy Dialogue on ‘Devolution of Powers and Good Governance in Pakistan’ at the University of Management and Technology in Lahore, he said the proposed “reset” did not mean a change of government or political party but a comprehensive review and restructuring of the administrative system to make it responsive to the needs of citizens. He even called for a debate on granting provincial status to Islamabad, saying residents of the federal capital did not receive a share under the National Finance Commission award. The development resulted in the PPP stepping up its opposition to the federal government’s statements on new provinces and administrative units. The PPP Sindh leadership, at a meeting chaired by provincial president Nisar Ahmed Khuhro the same day, accused the federal ministers of interfering in the constitutional affairs of the province and warned the federal government against any attempt to undermine Sindh’s autonomy or territorial integrity. The meeting called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to restrain his ministers from making statements on new provinces and warned that continued remarks could lead the PPP to conclude that the federal government was behind a “conspiracy against Sindh’s unity, provincial autonomy and the 18th Amendment”.

Despite a 2014 peace agreement, crime and violence continue to rack the Bangsamoro region in the southern Philippines. The military, which is still in charge of public safety, as well as the police and an array of local institutions are wrestling with outbreaks of fighting powered by easy access to firearms. Why does it matter? Local conflicts persist across the Bangsamoro, and the implementation of key provisions of the 2014 peace agreement remains well behind schedule. Entrenched clan feuds, political violence and criminal rackets make it hard to foster the trust in state institutions and social bonds needed to withstand future conflict. What should be done? Reforms to make regional law enforcement stronger, more professional and responsive to community needs are vital, as well as better coordination between the military and the police. Access to courts, control over firearms, and reinforced peacebuilding are also imperative to prevent the escalation of local violence and tackle its roots. Executive Summary The 2014 peace accord ended decades of conflict between the Philippine government and Moro Muslim separatists in what is now the Bangsamoro autonomous region. But violence still flares as clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal rackets rattle the region. The police struggle to keep pace, leaving the military as the dominant security force. Other institutions remain ill prepared for the challenge. Courts are slow and often fail to guarantee justice, while institutions tasked with maintaining peace in the region have been afflicted by political infighting between factions of the former insurgent movement, and have yet to become fully operational. A clearer division of responsibility between Manila and regional authorities, along with a broader recognition of the roots of local conflict and the recurrent outbreaks of violence they cause, will be crucial to improving security conditions. At the heart of these efforts should be a reform of the police, bolstering recruitment, internal discipline and community policing. Tighter gun control, targeted justice reforms and peacebuilding initiatives should complement these efforts. After decades of war between the Philippine government and Moro rebels, progress toward curbing violence in the Bangsamoro region since it became autonomous in 2019 has been patchy. While the largest armed movement in the region, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), has renounced armed struggle and shifted its attention to the regional parliament and government, flare-ups of competitive political violence now outweigh rebel or militant fighting with the state. Clan feuds and electoral rivalries drive vendettas that regularly displace entire communities and weaken state authority. Criminal rackets are rife and firearms are easy to get hold of, fuelling cycles of violence. Key aspects of the 2014 peace agreement, including its security provisions, remain unfulfilled. This includes rebel disarmament, but also the redeployment of the military to other parts of the country and the disarmament of private militias. One of the biggest challenges in the normalisation process, as the region’s transition from war to peace is officially called, remains policing. The issue of who should be in charge of maintaining peace and order was the subject of intense debate during peace talks and in crafting the region’s autonomy law. Granting the regional government authority to handle public security was one option, but in the end Manila retained policing power in the region. Even so, the national police has struggled to define its role in areas of the newly autonomous region that remain affected by violence. Meanwhile, the integration of Moro ex‑rebels into the police force has been painstakingly slow. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. In the absence of a credible and capable police force in the region, the Philippine armed forces are still the dominant security institution in the Bangsamoro. The military has earned public respect after decades of fighting a counterinsurgency in the area, but it is ill suited to handling local conflicts over the long run. Manila is grappling with how best to manage these dilemmas by continuing to deploy the military while using the police as backup. This approach, however, runs counter to the national government’s broader strategy of pivoting away from counterinsurgency to focus instead on external defence. For communities across the Bangsamoro hit by recurrent waves of violence, help is not always ready to hand. Communities often see the police as weaker, more politicised (especially due to local powerbrokers’ influence) and less dependable than the military. The regional government has greater powers over local dispute resolution and is in charge of building the local justice system, but is struggling to use its resources and is roiled by infighting. Long distances, case backlogs and steep costs mean local courts are often inaccessible to the Bangsamoro’s poorest citizens. The judiciary’s shortcomings are exacerbated by frequent score-settling between rival clans or bands, which can turn the filing of a legal case in court after a killing into the pretext for a fresh round of blood-letting and retaliation from the perpetrator’s clan. A rich tradition of community-based conflict resolution across the region offers alternatives, but its interaction with formal institutions has been uneven, and disputes often end up resurfacing. Both the national and regional governments should undertake reforms to mitigate violence and build a firmer foundation for handling threats to security. Supporting and professionalising the police is critical, but building a credible force will depend on practical improvements rather than sweeping reforms. Sustained efforts to rethink force structure, training and anti-corruption initiatives would help create a service responsive to the region’s needs. The police should also work to build better relations with communities, above all by addressing their most urgent concerns. Recruiting and training community safety police officers could be one way of bridging that gap. Ensuring better coordination between the military and police is also imperative. One solution would be for the military to gradually step back, enabling the police to take on more responsibilities for the management of public order. The relative calm in parts of the region should make this shift possible in at least some areas. These innovations should be accompanied by institutional reforms. The Bangsamoro needs sturdier mechanisms for settling disputes. Judicial reforms are also essential. For now, the formal justice system in the Bangsamoro remains weak, slow and too hard for its citizens to access, undermining public confidence in the courts. Strengthening Bangsamoro courts of all kinds with resources and personnel is paramount. Lastly, there are simply too many guns in the region for its citizens to be safe. Deterring gun use and clamping down on the supply of illegal weapons are essential to halt firearms proliferation. Together, these reforms should help curb the drivers of local violence, steer the region away from cycles of conflict and ensure law enforcement is in the hands of professional institutions that are responsive to the people of the Bangsamoro. Much as it was a singular achievement to end decades of insurgency, communities will not feel safe until the peace gets the policing it needs. Introduction For over five decades, a secessionist war raged in the Philippines’ southernmost island of Mindanao. The Muslim Moro people – who long experienced discrimination in the country – agitated for self-determination. 1 The term “Moro” refers to Islamised people in the southern Philippines, comprising thirteen ethno-linguistic groups. Two main armed movements representing Moro Muslim communities emerged: the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and its post 1977 splinter, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). 2 For earlier reporting on the peace process and transition, see Crisis Group Asia Reports N°355, Peace in the Philippines: The Bangsamoro’s Moment of Truth ; N°331, Southern Philippines: Making Peace Stick in the Bangsamoro , 1 May 2023; N°323, Islamist Militancy in the Southern Philippines , 18 March 2022; N°322, Southern Philippines: Fostering an Inclusive Bangsamoro , 18 February 2022; N°313, Southern Philippines: Keeping Normalisation on Track in the Bangsamoro , 15 April 2021; and N°306, Southern Philippines: Tackling Clan Politics in the Bangsamoro , 14 April 2020. The Philippine government deployed its military, paramilitary auxiliaries, and police against these groups. Over 120,000 people died in a conflict that did huge harm to public trust in state institutions and propagated the spread of weapons across numerous communities. The 2014 peace accord between Manila and the MILF – which provided political and fiscal autonomy to the Moro people within the boundaries of the Philippine state – marked a vital step toward reconciliation. In 2018, the Philippine Congress passed the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which voters then endorsed in a two-stage plebiscite in early 2019, thereby creating the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The Bangsamoro Transition Authority, an interim government led by the MILF, assumed power that February. The interim authority exercises self-governance in the Bangsamoro region, home to more than four million people spread across five provinces. The peace agreement foresaw two parallel tracks to achieve full Bangsamoro autonomy. First, former rebels would run the interim regional administration, pass new laws and build institutions. This political track was meant to conclude with regional elections in 2022, but these have been postponed several times, and are now planned for September 2026. Secondly, a “normalisation” agenda was to guide the broader transition from war to peace; it includes issues such as rebel disarmament but also socio-economic development and policing in the region. 3 The normalisation process does not have a set deadline and instead relies on qualitative milestones; both sides are meant to sign an “Exit Agreement” after they have met their respective commitments. As with the political track, however, the normalisation process has fallen behind schedule. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Achieving durable peace remains difficult in part because of deep social divisions. Kinship networks, entrenched political clans, diverse ethnolinguistic identities, and the uneasy coexistence of emerging political parties with armed movements all shape the region’s public life. Talking about his movement’s transition from guerrilla warfare to governance, a senior MILF commander admitted: “It was easier in the jungle”. 4 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Political tensions have also flared within the former insurgency. In March 2025, Manila replaced the region’s chief minister, MILF Chairman Murad Ebrahim, with the organisation’s military chief, Abdulraof Macacua. This change fractured the movement, pitting commanders and cadres loyal to the Central Committee against Macacua’s faction. 5 Murad is closely aligned with MILF’s chief negotiator and head of its implementing panel Mohagher Iqbal, who wields substantial influence over the movement’s political cadres. In response to Macacua’s perceived violations of internal regulations, the Central Committee suspended both him and eight loyal senior commanders from their roles, stopping short of expelling them from the organisation. The Bangsamoro region governs itself – the interim government, for example, exercises control over public finances – but the state’s use of force remains under Manila’s control. Specifically, the national government retains command over the police, while the armed forces play an active role in ensuring security. This arrangement reflects the national government’s enduring caution about a region with a long history of rebellion and the Philippine constitution, which mandates just one police force. 6 Crisis Group interviews, Manila, 8 May 2026. See also Article XVI, Section 6 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Building on Crisis Group’s earlier work in the Bangsamoro, this report explores how public security is managed in the region, with particular attention to policing. It draws on years of field research in the Bangsamoro and Manila, including over 80 interviews with police and military officers, MILF commanders, representatives of the interim regional government, national and local officials, civil society figures, clan leaders, donors, villagers and decommissioned fighters. Women comprised around a third of interviewees. II. The Peace Deal and its Violent Aftermath Despite the undeniable progress made since the 2014 peace agreement, the Bangsamoro continues to grapple with security dilemmas. Although large-scale fighting has stopped, more than a third of young people across the region have experienced armed conflict within or near their homes since 2019. 7 Bangsamoro Youth Commission, “Bangsamoro Youth Assessment Study”, 2024, p. 60. A local civil society leader described the region as being in a state of “controlled peace”. 8 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 13 February 2026. Navigating sporadic outbursts of disorder remains particularly challenging for law enforcement. A. Conflict and Crime The national government now faces two main security threats in Mindanao. Its first concern are jihadist groups that have stayed out of the peace process and continue to fight the state. With the regional government’s support, Manila has managed to subdue cells from these outfits in the Sulu archipelago and contain groups in Central Mindanao. 9 Crisis Group interview, MILF commander, Cotabato City, 2 November 2023. The regional government has several programs to support fighters who gave up arms, and the MILF also played a role in influencing young Moros to cease armed struggle. But while their attacks on security forces have declined, these groups have not been decimated. 10 On 14 December 2025, a shooting at Sydney’s Bondi Beach claimed the lives of fifteen people at the hands of father and son, Sajid and Naveed Akram. In the weeks leading up to the attack, the duo had spent several weeks in Davao City in eastern Mindanao. While some investigative journalists suggested the journey was an attempt to establish ties with local jihadist networks, their precise motives for the trip remain unconfirmed. Crisis Group phone interviews, December 2025. Some locals fear that former militants could re-emerge. 11 Crisis Group interview, member of a peacebuilding non-governmental organisation from Maguindanao del Sur, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Remnants of the nationwide communist insurgency, the New People’s Army, also operate in parts of the region, particularly Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte. 12 Crisis Group Report N°338, Calming the Long War in the Philippine Countryside , 19 April 2024. According to government statistics, the insurgency numbers less than 1,000 fighters and no longer has any large units combining political cadres and fighters. Manila has looked to the military to patrol areas where these waning insurgencies persist. Meanwhile, the police take the lead in handling law and order in calmer areas, where guerrilla presence is negligible. Another obstacle to durable peace revolves around violent disputes over land and politics that have long plagued the region. Some of those are clan feuds, known as rido , and others are communal conflicts. These types of conflict are collectively referred to as “horizontal violence” by journalists and academics. 13 Crisis Group interview, civil society activist, Cotabato City, 26 March 2026. Clan feuds are comparable to vendettas. The number of shootings, particularly in Central Mindanao (Cotabato City, Maguindanao del Sur and parts of Lanao del Sur), is such that one parliamentarian described the atmosphere as “pervasive lawlessness”. 14 Crisis Group interview, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 17 February 2026. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, has recorded hundreds of incidents since January 2026 alone. See “Safeguard the Bangsamoro Vote: A critical period to transcend violence in the region”, Climate Conflict Action Asia, 30 July 2026. With many local disputes escalating into large-scale clashes, the failures of both the military and police to deter shootings have become conspicuous. The upcoming parliamentary elections are likely to aggravate tensions, as rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disturb the ballot. 15 Crisis Group interview, Bangsamoro political strategist, 28 April 2026, Manila. The three local elections held in the region since its creation – in 2022, 2024 and 2025 – were less volatile than in the past but still featured high levels of violence. Infighting within the MILF is also a source of tension. 16 Crisis Group interviews, community leaders and officials, Cotabato City, 5-6 August 2026. While certain disputes stem from local resource control, deepening rifts within the MILF drive other conflicts. Frequently, these dynamics intertwine as factionalism amplifies existing land conflicts. Crisis Group interview, conflict researcher, Manila, 13 August 2026. Violence escalates quickly and frequently recurs in the region’s most conflict-affected areas, with outbreaks occurring most recently in the Special Geographic Area and parts of Maguindanao del Sur. 17 An ambush on Bangsamoro’s Chief Minister Macacua in the village of Bitu in Maguindanao del Norte by unidentified gunmen further highlighted the region’s volatility. The attack did not hurt anyone in Macacua’s convoy. Edwin Fernandez, “BARMM chief survives ambush in Maguindanao”, Inquirer , 16 August 2026. Criminal activity in the Bangsamoro also thrives wherever state authority is weak. While petty crimes such as theft or robberies are relatively rare in the region, illicit economies are ubiquitous, and have evolved in parallel to the peace process. 18 Crisis Group interviews, observers and police officers, February-March 2026. Kidnappings for ransom, which used to be Mindanao’s most lucrative business, have almost disappeared; smuggling, however, has proliferated, including for goods ranging from weapons to cooking oil. 19 Maritime Bangsamoro in particular, especially the provinces of Tawi-Tawi and Basilan, along with its former province Sulu, has traditionally been Mindanao’s “backdoor”, where many local communities have long treated smuggling to and from the Malaysian state of Sabah as legitimate commerce. In Central Mindanao, illicit cigarette trading has also flourished, much of it supplied from Indonesia and Vietnam and allegedly shielded by local powerbrokers. Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026; diplomats, Manila, 30 April 2026. See also, United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, “ An Interconnected Criminal Ecosystem: Transnational Organized Crime Threat Assessment for South-East Asia ”, July 2026, pp. 216-217. This illicit activity, however, has not led to open violence between competing criminal interests as syndicates appear to work with local governments rather than against them, and turf wars are scarce. Human trafficking across the region, especially involving women, also remains a concern given the region’s porous borders and long coastlines. 20 See for example, Lean Bolongon, “Safeguarding minors: Combating illegal recruitment in BARMM”, Philippine Information Agency , 17 March 2026. Another profitable business in Mindanao is the drug trade. During former President Rodrigo Duterte’s term in office from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine police carried out a nation-wide anti-drug campaign that targeted suspected dealers and users, killing thousands. 21 Georgi Engelbrecht, “Philippines: The International Criminal Court Goes After Duterte’s Drug War”, 17 September 2021. While some Mindanao drug lords were killed, other networks survived and have since flourished. 22 Crisis Group interview, security analyst, Manila, 10 March 2026. As early as 2023 – just a year after Duterte left office – a local activist in Marawi declared that the “drugs are back”. 23 Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 26 October 2023. The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency and the police continue counter-narcotic operations; some locals say they have recently seen an increase in arrests and shoot-outs. 24 Crisis Group has recorded at least ten such anti-drug operations across the region in 2026 so far. One clash in August between security forces and an armed drug trafficking outfit in Bongao town in Tawi-Tawi left one person dead and three others wounded, including a naval officer. 25 Edwin Fernandez, “PDEA agent, drug suspect killed; 3 Marines wounded in Tawi-Tawi”, Inquirer , 9 August 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power. The proliferation of firearms has also contributed to conflict and crime in the region. 26 It is notoriously hard to determine the total number of guns in the region. In late 2024, the police estimated that the region had over 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a well-informed interlocutor told Crisis Group that there were 20,000 legally registered ones. Crisis Group interview, 11 February 2026. In the Bangsamoro, as well as in other regions where the state’s security apparatus is weak or corrupted, guns are viewed as symbols of status and power; decades of war have made weapons ubiquitous. 27 Individuals and clans carry a wide variety of weapons, ranging from antiquated rifles to machine guns. Other Philippine regions where guns are prevalent are Abra and Negros. Members of armed groups and many local politicians, civilians and ex-combatants carry these weapons. 28 The first armed movement in the region, the MNLF, despite having splintered into factions, also retains weapons. The 1996 peace agreement with the movement sidestepped the question of disarmament, but in the absence of any attacks on government forces by a MNLF faction since 2012, Manila tolerates the awkward status quo of hundreds of MNLF fighters still being under arms. Crisis Group interviews, MNLF political cadre, Cotabato City, 16 February 2026. Under the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has taken part in the gradual demobilisation of its forces. In early 2026, however, the group stopped formally participating in the process and other normalisation activities such high-level meetings due to Manila’s perceived failure to fulfil promises of socio-economic benefits for combatants who lay down their arms; 14,000 fighters have still to be decommissioned, along with 2,450 weapons. 29 Taher Solaiman, “MILF declares ‘temporary pause’ in peace process engagement with national government”, Luwaran.com , 17 March 2026. Following discussions between its peace panel and government counterparts, the MILF ended the temporary suspension of its engagement in the peace process in early August, but demobilisation of rebels appears to still be on hold. 30 Carolyn Arguillas, “GPH-MILF Peace Implementing Panels finally meet; MILF’s ‘temporary pause’ lifted”, Mindanews , 5 August 2026. While there has been a proliferation of Philippine gun laws over the past five decades, they are strikingly permissive. Under a so-called Type 5 licence, for example, Filipinos are allowed to possess up to fifteen firearms. Existing ordinances, moreover, are loosely enforced. Individuals often acquire weapons legally but then remove their serial numbers, making them untraceable. 31 Crisis Group interview, police officer, Manila, 10 May 2026. Consequently, the government’s main focus is on the pool of “loose” firearms – those guns which the state cannot trace or document – with the goal of either seizing them or persuading politicians and civilians to turn them in. 32 The term “loose firearms” refers broadly to weapons that rebels, criminals or civilians hold without proper registration, including those purchased legally but later left unregistered or with expired licenses. But the task is overwhelming; civil society activists say guns continue to flow in and out of the Bangsamoro without any means to trace them. 33 Crisis Group phone interview, source from Basilan, 28 February 2026. High-calibre weapons such as mortars, machine guns or assault rifles can easily stoke local conflicts as their lethality increases the likelihood of casualties and tit-for-tat retaliation. 34 On 2 August, national police chief Jose Nartatez pushed for a crackdown on illegal firearms and armed groups in the region ahead of the September polls. Andrea Gregorio, “PNP ramps up ops vs gun-for-hire groups ahead of BARMM polls”, Inquirer , 2 August 2026. For its part, the interim regional government has only recently started discussing a bill to regulate firearms and ammunition in the autonomous region. 35 Member of parliament Omar Sema filed the bill on 16 April 2026, marking the sole instance that such legislation has been discussed in the regional parliament, out of the 469 bills it has passed so far. In the meantime, local governments such as the province of Basilan have launched programs to collect small arms and light weapons. This effort is being done in coordination with the national peace process office and is underwritten by foreign donors. Buy-in, however, has been uneven. 36 An obstacle to these schemes is that the market value of firearms often surpasses the cash incentives offered to rebels or civilians for surrendering them. Two senior military commanders expressed deep scepticism about the campaign, arguing that the initiative would have no meaningful impact on the security landscape, was far too modest in scale, and targeted the wrong weapons (those not in the hands of rebels or ex-combatants). Crisis Group interviews, Maguindanao and Cotabato, February-March 2026. Other proposed solutions, such as forced mass disarmament or the comprehensive registration of firearms, do not seem realistic in the Bangsamoro context. 37 Crisis Group interviews, interim government officials and civil society representatives, Cotabato City, February-March 2026. Efforts to create “zones of peace” or “gun-free zones”, often initiated by non-government organisations, have been short-lived. 38 Crisis Group interview, head of a civil society organisation, Cotabato City, 9 February 2026. Policing under Autonomy To meet the challenge of the post-conflict landscape, the drafters of the 2014 peace agreement had to think hard about the best way to police the region. 39 During the peace talks, policing was a key subject – as contentious as it was during negotiations between the government and the MNLF in 1996. That peace agreement contained no provisions for disarmament or demobilisation, and clashes continued to flare more than a decade after the deal. While the 1996 agreement envisaged integrating MNLF rebels into state forces, only a quarter of the insurgent force eventually joined the police or military, voluntarily bringing with them more than 4,000 firearms Crisis Group interview, military officer, Manila, 26 February 2026. See also, Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, “Integration of MNLF forces into the PNP and AFP: Integration without demobilization and disarmament”, unpublished paper for UP Center on Integrative and Development Studies project on the GRP-MNLF peace agreement, 2000. The agreement called for a regional police force that was to be “civilian in character, effective and efficient in law enforcement, fair and impartial, and accountable under the law for its actions”, and whose mandate would be “law enforcement and maintenance of peace and order” in the region. 40 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro and Annex on Normalisation . But the division of labour between Manila, its national police force and the region remained ambiguous. 41 The Philippine National Police, created in 1991, is tasked with preventing and investigating criminal activities and strengthening internal security. The Department of Interior and Local Government has political control over the force, while the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) administers and disciplines it. The president selects the national police chief and senior police officers and appoints the secretary of the department of interior and local government. Headquartered in Manila, the force maintains regional, provincial and municipal stations across the archipelago, but also includes two specialised units: the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group focuses on organised crime and terrorism; the Special Action Force, the PNP’s elite commando unit, is in charge of counterterrorism, hostage rescue, and high-risk operations as well as ad hoc tasks such as patrolling hot spots during elections. One part of the agreement stipulated that the regional government, working in coordination with Manila, “shall have primary responsibility over public order and safety within the Bangsamoro”. 42 Annex on Power Sharing , Art. II, 14. In another part, the accord said the police force is “responsible both to the central government and the Bangsamoro government”. 43 Framework Agreement and Annex on Normalisation. The Philippine Constitution is clear in that regard, as Art. 10 Section 21 states: “The preservation of peace and order within the regions shall be the responsibility of the local police agencies which shall be organised, maintained, supervised, and utilised in accordance with applicable laws. The defence and security of the regions shall be the responsibility of the National Government”. Government officials involved in the negotiations say the agreement was clear the regional police would remain under national authority. 44 One official involved in the process, however, said that Manila dodged the hard questions until the end, keeping the wording intentionally vague, and ended up “parking” the issue for the future. Crisis Group interview, Manila, 31 July 2026. The MILF, however, maintains that the common understanding in talks was that policing should be under the control of the autonomous government. The agreement also set up an Independent Commission on Policing to determine how law enforcement should function in the new region. When the commission delivered its report in April 2014, it recommended that the force remain a part of the national police, but stressed that it should invest in community‑based policing. 45 The Independent Commission on Policing for the Bangsamoro, “Policing for the Bangsamoro”, 2014. Report on file with Crisis Group. Community policing is generally understood as an approach that builds active partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to solve community problems and jointly ensure public safety. The commission highlighted the need for community policing that respects human rights and Sharia law. Another problem the commission identified was the police’s weak accountability to the communities they serve. Tasked with translating the occasionally vague peace agreement into clear and legally binding terms, the 2019 autonomy law dismissed the idea of a separate Bangsamoro police force. Wary of clashing with the 1987 constitution’s centralised approach to policing, lawmakers assigned public order and safety to the national government. 46 A single national police force was mandated to curb the historical misuse of local law enforcement by warlords. Yet mindful of the authoritarian practices during Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos, the constitution balanced this by granting local governments a supervisory role to ensure checks and balances. This outcome reflected the stance of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who was in office when the autonomy law came into force, but both the national police force and lawyers were also sceptical about proposals for a separate regional police force. 47 Crisis Group telephone interview, analyst, 18 February 2021. In early 2019, the national police established a Police Regional Office (PRO-BARMM), which is part of the national police and therefore firmly under Manila’s control. 48 According to most observers and local figures, any change to this status quo needs constitutional amendments. Crisis Group written communication, 12 June 2026. See also, Nash Maulana, “‘BARMM police, Moro Senate seat require Charter change”, Manila Standard , 3 May 2026. At the same time, the organic law included two compromise provisions. The first one was to allow the integration of MILF and MNLF members into PRO-BARMM (see Section III.A.2). 49 The MILF was critical towards integration of their forces into the police during the peace talks. Later, however, the movement accepted this provision in the autonomy law. The second one called for the chief of the regional police force to be appointed “upon consultation with the Chief Minister”. In practice, however, it is the national police chief who has ultimately decided on this appointment. 50 Crisis Group interview, government official, Manila, 27 February 2026. In late 2025, however, a national police commission resolution reiterated that the region’s chief minister can both recommend candidates and provide feedback on shortlisted officers. III. Security and Justice in Transition Various bodies in the Bangsamoro region are responsible for tackling flare-ups of violence. While the police and military remain central to maintaining order, other government and community institutions also help dispense justice and mediate disputes. A. The Police during the Bangsamoro Transition As is the case with the national police as a whole, the Bangsamoro force is hierarchical in nature. Its regional headquarters are in Parang, from which it oversees five provincial headquarters and more than one hundred municipal police stations. Every town has a team of officers who mostly take care of basic law enforcement. These tasks include investigating crimes, preparing requests for warrants or subpoenas from the courts, dealing with minor offences and arresting criminals and insurgents. 51 Arrest powers remain outside the military’s purview, except in instances of “in flagrante delicto” where troops directly witness a crime. The number of officers in the region is, by many accounts, insufficient: a regular station typically has a staff of a bit over twenty, covering municipalities with populations as large as 25,000. Overall, the police force’s headcount stands at over 7,000. 52 Crisis Group interviews, police officers, Cotabato City and Parang, 6-7 August 2026. Every municipal police chief shapes the local force’s policies on everything from community engagement and collaboration with politicians to defining how to handle local conflicts. In the post-2019 transition period, the police has emphasised anti-drug operations and curbing the spread of illegal firearms. 53 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. These priorities stem from the national government’s priority of combating drugs, as well as community support for the campaign. 54 Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Cotabato City, 6 August 2026. Given their limited numbers and lack of equipment, it has been more difficult for the police to address complex clan feuds, which can flare up without forewarning. In the most conflict-affected parts of Maguindanao, the police struggle to conduct even routine patrols, leaving law and order in the military’s hands. 55 A police chief from the region distinguished between “law enforcement”, for which the police is in the lead, and “combat operations” that are the domain of the military. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 17 February 2026. A senior police officer said the force can take care of so-called “soft targets”, but still need back-up if the operation occurs in a “harsh” context. 56 Crisis Group interview, Shariff Aguak, Maguindanao del Sur, 27 March 2026. According to one regional bureaucrat, the police may be willing to take over internal security but is currently “not capable” of doing so. Crisis Group interview, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Perceptions of law enforcers vary. The police appear more connected to everyday life than the military because their stations are located near town halls, making them visibly present. Some officers have a genuine desire to help their communities. But for many young Moro men and women, becoming a police officer is more about acquiring a secure job than answering the call of duty. 57 Crisis Group interview, member of parliament, Datu Odin Sinsuat, 13 February 2026; academic, Marawi City, 27 March 2026. Some locals are also sceptical about the ability of the police to respond to incidents. 58 In Lanao del Sur, a civil society activist also observed the police are too slow to respond to violence. Crisis Group interview, Marawi City, 14 February 2026. Locals in predominantly non-Moro Indigenous communities also feel that law enforcement does not always respond to their concerns. 59 Crisis Group interview, phone interview, community leader, 6 December 2021; online communication, peace process observer, 17 August 2026. That said, several surveys show the police enjoy a degree of trust from local people. 60 Crisis Group interview, Manila, 20 March 2026. Surveys made available to Crisis Group. Other survey data suggests that many residents continue to look to local leaders and religious figures for security. Tatsuya Koyama, “Who Supports the Peace? A Survey of Postconflict Public Opinion in Maguindanao, the Philippines”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 44 no. 3 (December 2025). At the beginning of the transition, many MILF commanders hoped community policing – namely, building partnerships between law enforcement and local citizens to ensure public safety – would become widespread. 61 Crisis Group interview, senior MILF commander, Cotabato City, 27 November 2019. The Philippine police have used civilian auxiliaries known as the Barangay Peace Action Teams (BPATs) and Civilian Volunteer Organisations (CVOs) that came closest to community policing. With police approval, BPATs may carry light firearms. CVOs focus on intelligence gathering, neighbourhood patrols, and emergency response. Officially unarmed, they may use weapons when supporting police operations, although in practice some mayors or village heads have been known to issue them firearms. Despite the support of international donors, however, and its inclusion in the Philippine policing doctrine, this approach never really gained momentum. 62 Crisis Group interview, donor official, Cotabato City, 11 February 2026. Police officers admit that resource limitations, understaffing and local politics complicate the work of fostering stronger relations with Bangsamoro communities. 63 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato and Parang, 5-7 August 2026. Even so, some individual officers have been more proactive. A former police chief in Maguindanao, for example, instructed his officers to visit communities and engage residents on important concerns, at times accompanied by representatives from the judicial system. 64 This community outreach mostly relates to drugs and firearms use. Crisis Group interview, senior police officer, Shariff Aguak, 27 March 2026. As for efforts to integrate MILF fighters into the police force, as stipulated in the autonomy law (see Section II.B), these have so far had limited success. In 2019, the government waived height, age, and education requirements for five years to allow more former MILF (and MNLF) rebels to qualify for recruitment in the regional force. After a two-year interruption due to the COVID-19 pandemic, 11,075 applicants took a special eligibility exam in May 2022, which 7,145 passed. Yet in the years that followed, the government earmarked only about 400 positions for the former fighters, and just 396 joined the police force. 65 At present, 36 women were considered for recruitment and have undergone on-the-job-training in police stations across the region. “The Peace Accords Matrix – Mindanao (PAM-M) and Civil Society Normalization Update Report (January-April 2026)”, University of Notre Dame, 3 August 2026, p. 11. While the interim government stepped in to fund their training, Manila subsequently grew sceptical of maintaining dedicated quotas for ex-rebels, and future applicants will have to compete within the general pool of all Filipinos vying for the 1,500 police positions available annually. 66 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. A small concession was a resolution by the national police commission in July 2025, which extended the police application deadline for MILF and MNLF members to 8 June 2027. Bong Sarmiento, “MILF, MNLF members who want to become cops can apply until June 2027”, Inquirer , 17 July 2025. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. While they may not have joined in large numbers, the former MILF fighters now working as police officers appear to have integrated smoothly. 67 Crisis Group interview, Manila, international observer, 21 October 2022. Police officers from Cotabato City said MILF recruits have been well‑received by their new colleagues, and a sense of camaraderie now animates the ranks. 68 Crisis Group interviews, Cotabato City, 28 March 2026, 6 August 2026. The Third Party Monitoring Team – an independent body mandated with overseeing the peace process – has encouraged further recruitment, underlining it “could serve as a powerful symbol of previously warring entities working constructively to build a secure future together”. 69 Third Party Monitoring Team, 9th public report, 5 May 2026, p. 61. But prospects for further integration appear dim. Manila has demonstrated no appetite to reintroduce a quota for ex-rebels or hire Moro who passed the exam but were not incorporated into the force. A part of the MILF, furthermore, still expects the regional government to take over policing in the region in the long term. 70 Crisis Group interview, international observer, Manila, 14 October 2022. Crisis Group interviews, MILF officials, February-March 2026. In this sense, the policing issue is emblematic of a broader lack of agreement on the future of the peace process. 71 Crisis Group interviews, international and local observers, Cotabato and Manila, February-March 2026. Marking its new secretary’s first 100 days, the Philippine peace process office’s late-July report made no mention of policing. Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity, July 2026. A mural near the regional police headquarters in Parang, Philippines. August 2026.
